- A bottle of flammable liquid in Poland, a nuclear option on a Russian wish-list—the hunt for Starlink widens
- Russia’s answer to Starlink was written off as a failure—its satellites are still climbing

articles.title: Iran plans to expand missile range to reach ‘enemy located at greater distance’, spokesperson says
articles.body:
The Iranian military will work to develop more missiles with a range exceeding 1000 kilometers, to reach “enemies at a greater distance from our forces.” Mohammad Akrami-Nia, spokesperson for the Islamic Republic’s Army, told the IRGC-affiliated Fars News Agency on Sunday.
Referring to the deployment of US military forces outside the Strait of Hormuz, he shared that “during this war, we reached the conclusion that we definitely need to increase the range of our missiles, and we have now moved in this direction.”
Iranian officials claimed in February that Tehran had deliberately capped the range of its missiles at 2,000 km to avoid being perceived as an international threat. Despite comments by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, reports in March said Tehran had attempted to strike Diego Garcia with two intermediate-range ballistic missiles, which would have required a range far beyond 2,000 km.
“The missiles that we used during the war, particularly those used by our ground forces to target enemy bases, which were used in Kuwait, and our naval forces also used naval missiles, or sea-launched missiles, sea cruise missiles, against enemy vessels,” he said.
“These were actually very good and effective missiles, and we have now reached the conclusion that we need to increase their speed and range, because the enemy is located at a greater distance from our forces. They are located at a distance of up to 1,000 kilometers, and God willing, we will upgrade them as well.”
Iran already possesses several missiles capable of traveling more than 1,000 km, including the Khorramshahr, a liquid-fueled medium-range ballistic missile with a reported range of up to 2,000–3,000 km; the Sejjil, a solid-propellant medium-range ballistic missile capable of striking targets roughly 2,000 km away; and the Shahab-3, a foundational medium-range ballistic missile with a reported range of up to around 1,300 km, capable of reaching Israel and parts of the wider region. Later variants of the Shahab-3, including the Ghadr-1, have reported ranges of up to roughly 1,950 km.
Iran claims attacks forced out US troops
The spokesperson’s claims came after IRGC Rear Admiral Ali Fadavi alleged that Iranian attacks forced the US military out of the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters.
In comments made to Iranian state media IRIB, Fadavi alleged on Sunday that “The Americans fled and moved more than 1,000 kilometers away from our borders. This was not their choice; it was due to the authority of the Islamic Republic and the authority of the IRGC Ground Force.”
“The Americans must use their vessels because you cannot exercise full sovereignty with air power. You can bomb the region every day, but unless your forces have a physical presence, you cannot impose your will,” he continued, going on to deny that the Islamic Republic targets assets and infrastructure of Islamic nations.
“...Any base belonging to the Americans, any vessel belonging to the Americans, will be targeted by the grace of God.”

articles.title: Ukraine scrambles for money to fight war as Russian strikes batter economy
articles.body:
Ukraine scrambles for money to fight war as Russian strikes batter economy
KYIV, Oct 5 - Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, is struggling to survive. Russian airstrikes have brought the city's huge steel plant and mines to a standstill, dragging the local economy to its knees.
Mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said the sprawling industrial city — which stretches along the banks of the Inhulets River — was doing everything possible to ensure its hospitals remain open, the lights remain on in kindergartens and schools, and buses keep running.
"In Kryvyi Rih, the situation is actually worse than anywhere else, apart from the front line itself," Vilkul, 52, a former mining executive, said in a video address.
The financial squeeze on the city of about 600,000 people underlines the challenges facing Ukraine as the government navigates its biggest budget crisis since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Last month, the city's largest employer — ArcelorMittal's hulking mining and steelmaking complex — suspended its operations following a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes that darkened its furnaces.
The prospects for next year, Vilkul said, are bleak.
"It's about survival. Right now, we need to survive," he said.
It's a scene played out across Ukraine's once-mighty steel industry, which accounted for a tenth of economic output before the war. Giant mills in Zaporizhzhia in the southeast and other industrial cities stand silent and exports have stopped.
An escalation in Russia's drone and missile strikes this summer destroyed factories and warehouses across Ukraine, damaged ports and railways, and forced shops and businesses to close, slowing the growth of the economy and tax revenue.
Meanwhile, the technology-driven war is becoming ever more expensive for Ukraine to fight.
Billions of euros in foreign loans have been delayed by failure to pass bills including unpopular tax reforms and anti-corruption legislation demanded by Ukraine's Western allies, leaving a gaping hole in state coffers.
Ukraine needs $56 billion to fund that gap this year —equivalent to about a quarter of its economic output. Of that, $27 billion is military spending.
To bridge the shortfall, Ukrainian officials met European partners in Brussels last week to discuss bringing forward disbursements due next year under a €90-billion ($101-billion) EU loan. The European Commission and Ukraine said they had identified funds to close the gap this year.
But three sources familiar with the talks said accelerating these payments risked increasing budget pressure next year - at a time when looming election campaigns in European allies including France and Poland could erode support for Kyiv.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi acknowledges the situation is "challenging". The government has been forced to freeze non-essential spending — including reconstruction of damaged buildings and infrastructure — to prioritise military spending, public sector wages and pensions.
"All resources should be channelled into critically important areas," Koretskyi told reporters.
WAR COSTS SOAR, DOMESTIC REVENUES FALL
Two years ago, a single day of fighting cost Ukraine $140 million, but that figure has jumped to $190 million, according to Roksolana Pidlasa, the head of parliament's budget committee. And that does not include direct military support to Kyiv from its Western allies.
Rising costs are driven partly by the need for expensive medium- and long-range weapons capable of striking Russia's oil refineries and military factories to reduce Moscow's ability to continue its war.
Plus, the wage bill for an expanded army is higher than ever before, and the state must support a growing number of military families of disabled or deceased soldiers.
"Expenditure will continue to rise," Pidlasa told a conference in Kyiv. "This is one more pragmatic reason why the US and Europe need to act faster to force (Russia) to end this war."
In the first nine months of this year, Ukraine spent more than $44 billion on defence alone, data showed. That does not include in-kind military support from allies.
In the same period, the government was able to raise only about $42 billion in tax revenue as the economy slowed.
Pidlasa said that in the first nine months of this year Ukraine's budget lost over 49.5 billion hryvnias ($1.1 billion) in tax revenue because of Russian attacks that not only damaged property and goods, but disrupted logistics and shut shops and businesses for hours at a time.
By the end of the year, the cumulative losses could rise to 70 billion hryvnias, the government estimates.
"We have not a temporary but a structural problem with the revenues at the very time when spending really requires resources," said Oleksandra Myronenko, an economist at the Centre for Economic Strategies, a Kyiv-based think tank.
Some Ukrainian businesses have started to scale back operations. Others have put capital expenditure on hold as the country braces for a difficult winter. Business sentiment and economic expectations are darkening.
Vasyl Khmelnytskyi, founder of an industrial park in the city of Bila Tserkva near Kyiv, said he had scrapped plans to build three new factories.
"The risks are simply too great right now — both for the business and for the people," he said in a Facebook post.
Ukraine's agricultural sector — its largest source of export revenues — has been particularly hard hit. Russian attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea ports led to a 36.6% fall in grain exports year-on-year in September.
About $40 billion in export revenue is at risk this year as a result of the blockade, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said.
Even with tens of billions of euros in foreign support, Ukraine's economy is expected to grow only between 0.5% and 1.5% this year, economists say — down from 1.8% in 2025.
FOREIGN AID IS DELAYED
During more than four years of intense fighting, Ukraine has been able to maintain macroeconomic and financial stability thanks to fiscal support from its Western partners, receiving nearly $200 billion since Russia's invasion.
But $29.5 billion in foreign aid is now at risk this year because of delays in passing reforms, Koretskyi said. The government has postponed about $900 million of capital spending until December, in the hope the legislation will be passed.
The aim is to pass all the required legislation in parliament by October 15, Koretskyi said.
"Only then we will get all the money," Koretskyi said. "This is absolutely vital. It needs to be done as soon as possible."
Legislators are now discussing the budget for next year. The government has proposed record defence budget spending of $110 billion. This figure does not include direct military aid.
Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko has estimated that the unfunded budget gap for the next year is already more than $32 billion.
Part of the solution, Marchenko said, is to use frozen Russian assets in Europe to fund Ukraine's budget. EU countries immobilised some €210 billion of Russian central bank assets after Moscow invaded Ukraine.
"Ukraine continues to mobilise domestic resources, but the scale of Russia's war puts clear limits on our capacity," Marchenko said on X. REUTERS

articles.title: Turkey weighs military support for Saudi Arabia under Mecca pact
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey weighs military support for Saudi Arabia under Mecca defence pact
Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan are set to hold high-level defence talks in Riyadh on Monday as Ankara signals its readiness to support the kingdom against continued Houthi attacks under the countries' newly signed joint defence pact.
Foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs from the three countries will attend a meeting of the Political and Defence Strategic Committee established under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on 7 August.
The talks come as Turkey steps up its engagement with Saudi Arabia amid growing questions over what military support Ankara could provide Riyadh, including expanding defence industry, intelligence cooperation and expertise in drone warfare.
Turkey's foreign ministry said Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of the General Staff Selcuk Bayraktaroglu would attend the meeting.
Fidan is expected to outline Turkey's position on consolidating the alliance and its next steps, as well as assess threats to peace and stability in the region and discuss developments impacting the three countries' shared security.
According to the ministry, Fidan will stress the importance of the alliance in providing a combined and effective response to threats and preventing regional crises.
He is also expected to reaffirm Turkey's "strong support" and solidarity with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks and stress that attacks targeting holy sites, including Mecca, are unacceptable.
Ankara is also expected to emphasise the importance of securing international trade routes and resolving regional conflicts through peaceful means.
Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Friday that Iran had proposed political engagement with the Houthis, an initiative expected to be discussed at the emergency Riyadh meeting.
Dar said Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan would determine their next steps during the talks.
The alliance is also expected to establish its secretariat in Riyadh, with Pakistan nominating retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood as its first secretary-general.
Mecca defence pact takes shape
The Political and Defence Strategic Committee, comprising the three countries' foreign and defence ministers and chiefs of staff, is responsible for directing activities under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
It held its first meeting in Istanbul on 31 August, when officials discussed the technical work required to institutionalise the alliance.
The countries' foreign ministers also met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where they discussed regional developments and issued a statement condemning attacks on Mecca, which the Houthis denied carrying out, as well as attacks on Saudi civilian and economic infrastructure.
The military chiefs of Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan subsequently met in Riyadh on 25 September.
Saudi Arabia's defence ministry said the commanders reviewed threats facing the kingdom and discussed strengthening military cooperation, intelligence sharing and coordination between their armed forces.
They also agreed to begin translating commitments under the Mecca pact into "effective military cooperation".
Fidan later said regional developments and military threats facing Saudi Arabia from both the north and south had been discussed.
He said Turkey's chief of staff had briefed President Recep Tayyip Erdogan following the technical military talks in Riyadh, adding that the Turkish armed forces possessed the capabilities and expertise required to respond to threats.
Erdogan has stressed that the pact should not be viewed as an alliance directed against Iran, Israel or any other country.
In an interview with Newsweek, he said the agreement was based on Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises the right to self-defence. Under the agreement, an armed attack against one of the three countries is considered an attack against all parties.
Erdogan said the response would depend on the requirements of the country under attack and could range from intelligence, logistical and ammunition support to broader military assistance.
What could Turkey provide?
Attention has increasingly turned to what Turkish support for Saudi Arabia could look like in practice.
Fidan said on 20 September that Ankara would consider Riyadh's military requirements as it confronted continuing attacks, while stressing that Saudi Arabia should not be drawn into the conflict between the United States and Iran.
Turkey's growing defence industry could become a central component of that support.
Ankara has developed significant capabilities in drones, missiles, smart munitions and artillery, while its armed forces have accumulated experience in conflicts involving armed groups and irregular forces.
Turkey provided extensive military support to Azerbaijan during the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war and intervened in support of Libya's internationally recognised government in 2019, where Turkish drones helped shift the military balance.
It has also conducted repeated military operations in northern Syria and Iraq and exported drones to countries including Ukraine and Ethiopia.
Those capabilities have prompted speculation that Ankara could provide Saudi Arabia with military advice, intelligence support and advanced weapons without becoming directly involved in fighting.
Ufuk Necat Tasci, a professor of international relations at Canakkale Onsekiz Mart University, told The New Arab that Fidan's comments signalled that Ankara was positioning itself firmly alongside Riyadh.
"Politically, this statement indicates that Turkey will enter the equation in favour of Saudi Arabia. Time will reveal whether this intervention will be direct or indirect," he said. "Nevertheless, Turkey does not want to remain neutral towards the attacks on Saudi Arabia during this period, because this alliance, as is clear, has raised concerns in both Israel and Iran."
Drones and air defence
Merve Suna Ozel Ozcan, an international relations academic at Kirikkale University, cautioned against interpreting Turkey's position as signalling direct military intervention.
"Fidan's statement should be interpreted from the perspective of solidarity, not war or aggression," she told TNA.
She noted that defence industry cooperation was among the clearest areas in which Ankara could assist Riyadh, particularly through drone technology.
Turkey and Saudi Arabia already have an agreement involving the Bayraktar Akinci combat drone, with Turkish defence company Baykar and Saudi military industries pursuing local production and technology transfer.
Ozcan said the nature of Houthi warfare meant Saudi Arabia required more than additional advanced air defence systems such as the Patriot and THAAD.
Riyadh also needed additional defensive layers, she said, particularly cheaper systems capable of countering large-scale drone attacks.
Such cooperation could offer the clearest indication yet of how the Mecca agreement will move from a political commitment to a functioning defence alliance, as Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan seek to define how collective defence will work in practice.

articles.title: Air defense downs 172 of 205 Russian targets, hits at 13 locations – Air Force
articles.body:
The Defense Forces of Ukraine neutralized 172 Russian targets on Monday night, though hits from Russia air attack weapons were recorded at 13 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense shot down/suppressed 172 Russian Shahed, Gerbera, and other types of UAVs," the report states.
Overall, on the night of October 5 (starting from 18:00 on October 4), Russia attacked with 205 strike UAVs of the Shahed type (49 of them jet-powered), Gerbera, Banderol/Dan-T, and decoy drones of the Parodia type from the directions of Oryol, Kursk, Shatalovo, Millerovo, Primorsko-Akharsk (Russia), temporarily occupied Donetsk, and temporarily occupied the Autonomous Republic of Crimea – Hvardiiske.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare (EW) units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
Meanwhile, impacts from Russian air attack weapons were recorded at 13 locations, along with the fall of shot-down debris at 3 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with about ten Russian UAVs remaining in the airspace, the command added.

articles.title: Ukraine and Germany Sign 15 Deals Worth €8.5B for Air Defense, Radars, and Interceptors
articles.body:

- War in Ukraine
Ukraine and Germany Sign 15 Deals Worth €8.5B for Air Defense, Radars, and Interceptors
Ukraine and Germany have reached 15 agreements worth more than €8.5 billion covering air defense, drone interceptors, missiles, radars, artillery, unmanned ground systems, and energy support, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said following talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy in a Telegram post on October 4, the 15 agreements cover drone interceptors, small missiles, radars, unmanned ground systems, artillery, air defense, Patriot missile production in Germany, and support for Ukraine’s energy sector.
“As of today, we have 15 agreements and documents with the German side, and most of them concern security cooperation, production, relevant procurement, our orders for German industry, and joint projects in Ukraine. The total value of our agreements today is more than €8.5 billion,” Zelenskyy said.
The agreements include cooperation on drone interceptors, small anti-drone missiles, radars, artillery, unmanned ground vehicles, and additional air defense capabilities. Kyiv and Berlin will also work to increase production in Germany of missiles used by Patriot air defense systems, according to the Presidential Office.
Ukraine has also placed a major order with German defense manufacturer Diehl Defence for IRIS-T air defense systems. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry signed three memoranda with Diehl covering IRIS-T systems and missiles as well as ammunition. Separate agreements were reached with Hensoldt on radar procurement and Quantum Systems on testing and supplying interceptor drones.
Zelenskyy also reported positive testing of the German-Ukrainian Spear interceptor. Work is continuing on another weapon, the Nika small missile, designed specifically to counter Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type drones and which has yet to undergo testing.
Germany separately announced a new support package for Ukraine worth more than €1.3 billion, which includes defense assistance and funding for Ukraine’s energy sector ahead of winter. Part of the funding will go toward producing new interceptors designed to engage jet-powered Russian attack drones.
“It includes weapons that will help us now, as well as support for our energy sector, which is very important, ahead of winter—an important energy package. This comprehensive package from Germany also includes funding for the production of new interceptors specifically against jet-powered ‘shaheds,’” Zelenskyy said.
Germany is also involved in FREYJA, a European anti-ballistic missile defense project led by Ukrainian company Fire Point, with Germany’s Hensoldt supplying radar technology. The system is expected to integrate FP-7.x interceptors, launchers, and TRML-4D radars.
The agreements also cover energy cooperation, including equipment for Ukraine’s power grid and projects with Siemens Energy involving gas turbines, infrastructure protection, and power generation.
The focus on faster interceptors comes as Russia increasingly uses jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which fly significantly faster than conventional propeller-driven variants and reduce the time available for interception. Zelenskyy said Russia launched around 900 jet-powered Shaheds in the week before Merz’s visit.

articles.title: Why the U.S. Bomber Withdrawal From a U.K. Air Base Is Significant
articles.body:
The U.S. over the weekend removed all of its B-1 Air Force bombers, thought to be around a dozen, from the RAF Fairford base in southern England, a week after several men were arrested nearby in relation to a suspected terror plot, which the U.K. government believes may be linked to Iran.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a U.S. Defense Department official told TIME, specifying that U.S. bombers “routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.” The official added that America’s bomber force remains “ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities… anywhere, anytime.”
A spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the RAF Fairford base remains safe, but refused to offer any specific comment on the military operations of “foreign nations.” The British Ministry of Defense directed TIME to the U.S. Air Force when approached for comment.
The Pentagon has not offered a specific reason behind the move, but it comes after five men, all U.K. nationals, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses on Sept. 27, following a suspected terror plot nearby RAF Fairford, an airbase used by the U.S. to strike Iran. Officers made the arrests after receiving a tip-off that three "suspicious vehicles" appeared to be heading toward the direction of the base. Amid ongoing investigations, British counterterrorism police arrested a dual British-Iranian national in central London on Oct. 1 on suspicion of terrorist acts in connection with the incident. All arrestees have been released on bail.
David Dunn, a professor of international politics at the University of Birmingham, says the U.S. withdrawal from Fairford is “historic, unprecedented, and an indication of the sense of vulnerability” surrounding U.S. military assets abroad.
“Fairford is normally the place during a crisis where America sends bombers to beef up America's military capability and its formal operating bases, whether that's for operations in Europe, like the Kosovo campaign, or for operations in the Gulf through 2003 onwards, or indeed for operations in Iran,” Dunn tells TIME. “This [removal] is an indication of concerns about the safety of those assets in their forward operating bases.”
Dunn adds “the haste” with which the operation took place over the weekend is also noteworthy, referencing reports that some of the aircraft had only been there for a relatively short period of time, having arrived recently as part of a rotation.
A report by the New York Times said U.S. commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford, citing two U.S. officials. TIME has been unable to independently verify these reports.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday dismissed the idea that the removal of U.S. bombers was directly connected to the foiled plot. He reiterated the U.S.’ stance that it’s “not unusual to see rotations happen” and said he has “confidence” in the security of U.S. bases, adding that the British “couldn’t be more cooperative” in the ongoing investigation regarding RAF Fairford.
U.K. and U.S. officials suspect Iranian involvement in RAF Fairford plot
Both U.K. and U.S. officials have voiced suspicion of Iranian involvement in the suspected terror plot.
Burnham on Sept. 30 said the U.K. believes Iran was likely involved in the incident.“There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation,” he said, adding that British forces were “working closely” with U.S. counterparts.
Iran has vehemently denied any involvement. In the immediate aftermath of the initial arrests, the Iranian embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any attempt to "link Iran to" the arrests made near RAF Fairford. After Burham’s comments, Iran doubled down on its denial, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accusing the U.K. of “barking up the wrong tree.”
President Donald Trump previously said the five men arrested at the scene had been under “investigation” prior to the arrests and were looking to cause “big damage.” Asked whether Iran was involved in the suspect terror plot, he said, “it might be,” but did not offer further details.
Dunn says that although Iran “hasn't got the range to [directly] attack bases in the U.K.,” it does not necessarily remove the potential threat to U.S. assets stationed there. “Iran—by doing things via proxies, organized criminal gangs, or hiring people gangs through payments through the dark web—can still have a military effect and a deterrent effect on the operation of a base like Fairford,” he says.
Counter Terrorism Policing has said it is looking at all angles, citing possible foreign-state involvement as one line of inquiry. It has urged against conclusions being drawn in what is a high-profile and active investigation.
How RAF Fairford has supported U.S. military operations for decades
RAF Fairford is a NATO-designated standby deployment and a U.S. forward operating base for U.S. Global Strike Command, according to U.K. government records. The base, which opened in 1944, has been used extensively by U.S. military aircraft in previous conflicts, including "Operation Iraqi Freedom" in 2003.
The U.S. Air Force describes RAF Fairford as its “preferred” European “bomber forward operating location” and previously said it has used Fairford “nearly continuously” since the base was constructed.
Former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer initially refused to allow U.S. access to U.K. military bases in its offensive strikes against Iran—a move that earned him the wrath of Trump. Starmer changed his position in March, authorizing the U.S. to use bombers based at RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned the base could be a target on account of its use by the U.S. military, insisting it makes the U.K. a “participant in aggression” in the war.
Starmer had previously warned the British public of the general threat posed by Iran. On Feb. 28, in an address to the nation hours after the U.S. and Israel launched its initial strikes against Iran, he said: “Even in the United Kingdom, the Iranian regime poses a direct threat to dissidents and the Jewish community. Over the last year alone, they have backed more than 20 potentially lethal attacks on U.K. soil.”

articles.title: Ukraine, Germany Sign €8.5B in Defense Deals, Merz Pledges More Air Defense Support
articles.body:
Kyiv and Berlin have agreed on joint weapons production, signing 15 contracts worth more than €8.5 billion ($9.5 billion), with a primary focus on air defense missiles and advanced drones.
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the agreements following a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The deals cover a range of defense priorities, including strengthening Ukraine’s artillery capabilities, protecting energy infrastructure, and countering Russian drones.
What the new agreements entail
Key areas of cooperation include the development of small missiles, radars, and ground-based robotic systems. The package also includes the FREYJA project and an expansion of German production capacity for ammunition for the Patriot air defense system.
Zelensky said the Ukrainian defense orders would provide work for German companies while significantly strengthening the defense industries of both countries.
“Germany is helping us during this war, and now Ukraine is placing defense and other orders that will create opportunities for German companies. This will make a significant contribution to Germany’s economy.”
The agreements were announced during Merz’s unannounced visit to Kyiv, which came as Russia intensified attacks on Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, Der Spiegel reported.
Merz arrived by special train alongside German Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche and a 10-member delegation of business and defense-industry executives.
Russia Repeatedly Tests Romanian Air Defense
Speaking at Kyiv’s central railway station, Merz stressed that European security was directly tied to Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russia.
“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.
Merz also reaffirmed Berlin’s commitment to supporting Ukraine, saying Kyiv could “continue to count on our help” as Russian attacks intensify ahead of the heating season.
According to German government officials cited by Der Spiegel, Merz plans to guarantee the rapid delivery of 1,000 newly developed interceptor systems designed to destroy jet-powered Shahed drones.
The visit came days after Merz described Ukraine’s air defense as its “weakest point” and said Germany was working with European partners to assemble additional military support ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15-16.
Merz has repeatedly argued that continued military support for Ukraine is essential to European security.
In a recent speech in Münster, he warned that a peace dictated by Russia would destabilize Europe, trigger new refugee flows, and leave the continent vulnerable to further Russian pressure.
His visit also came amid growing political tensions at home. Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which opposes arms deliveries to Ukraine and calls for the resumption of Russian gas imports, has made significant electoral gains, including strong results in recent state elections.

articles.title: Three Russian Officers Linked to Missile Strikes on Ukraine Killed in Tu-95 Crash
articles.body:
Three Russian officers linked by a Ukrainian database to the organization of missile strikes on Ukraine were among eight officers killed when a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in Russia’s Amur Region on Sept. 29, independent Russian outlet Mediazona reported.
The bomber crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo during a training flight from the Ukrainka airbase. Initial reports said six crew members were killed.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Mediazona later verified the identities of all eight people aboard and found that all had served in Russia’s strategic aviation forces. Six were members of the Tu-95MS’ regular crew, while two others may have been aboard as inspectors or passengers.
Three of the dead – Maj. Andrei Lobanov, Maj. Andrei Gerasimov and Lt. Col. Fyodor Pavlyukov – are listed by Ukraine’s “Book of Executioners of the Ukrainian People” project as participants in or organizers of Russian missile strikes on Ukrainian territory.
The project, launched after Russia’s full-scale invasion, maintains a database of Russian military personnel and other individuals it says are involved in crimes against Ukraine.
The information is collected and documented using publicly available data as well as information from Ukrainian law enforcement and intelligence agencies.
Mediazona said the three officers’ inclusion in the database links them specifically to Russia’s strategic aviation operations against Ukraine.
India Pushing for Bigger Role in Russia-Ukraine Talks
Most of the eight officers killed in the crash had previously served at the Engels airbase in Russia’s Saratov Region before being transferred to the Ukrainka base in Amur Region, Mediazona reported.
The Tu-95MS is one of Russia’s main strategic bombers used to launch long-range cruise missiles against targets across Ukraine.
The bombers were also among the key targets in the clandestine Ukrainian operation dubbed “Operation Spiderweb” in June 2025, in which dozens of Tu-95s on tarmacs were hit after Ukraine deployed drones that had been smuggled near airfields disguised as modular houses.

articles.title: Russia’s Jet Drones Kill 1, Injure 8 in Kharkiv Amid 205-Drone Overnight Barrage
articles.body:
Russia attacked Kharkiv late on Oct. 4 with three “Banderol” jet-powered drones, killing one person and injuring eight, including one critically, Mayor Ihor Terekhov reported.
The drones struck near residential buildings in the city’s Industrialnyi district, shattering windows in five buildings and damaging their roofs, Terekhov said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Unfortunately, there is one fatality. In addition, eight people were injured, one of whom is in critical condition,” he said.
Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, said one of the strikes hit a high-rise building.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported fires at an administrative building and an industrial facility. Several vehicles were also damaged.
According to Novosti.LIVE, the man killed in the attack was traveling in a car with a woman and a dog when the strike occurred. The woman survived but was taken to intensive care, while the dog was rescued from the vehicle and taken to an animal care center.
The Kharkiv strike came amid a large-scale Russian drone attack on Ukraine.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched 205 strike unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) against Ukraine from 6 p.m. on Oct. 4, including 49 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, as well as Gerbera, Banderol/Dan-T and Parodiya decoy drones.
Ukrainian forces countered the attack using aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems, as well as mobile fire groups.
Zelensky Vows Proportional Retaliation for Russian Bridge Strikes
As of 8 a.m. on Oct. 5, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 172 Russian drones, the Air Force reported.
“Impacts from enemy aerial assets were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at three other locations,” the report said.
The attack included the jet-powered Banderol drones that struck Kharkiv, where three drones hit near residential buildings in the Industrialnyi district, killing one person and injuring eight, according to Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov.
On the afternoon of Oct. 2, Russian forces attacked two districts of Kharkiv with guided aerial bombs. One of the bombs struck a private home, killing two people and injuring 42 others, including three children.
The attack damaged 23 private houses, an educational institution, office buildings, seven vehicles and power lines. Across the Kharkiv region, Russian strikes that day killed five people and injured 49, according to local authorities.
The latest air assault also comes amid warnings that Russia could intensify its attacks on major Ukrainian cities as winter approaches.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has previously warned that Russia could seek to isolate Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa from the rest of Ukraine through intensified attacks. He has also said Lviv, a key logistics hub near the Polish border, could become a target.
Zelensky said he had information that Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the removal of restrictions on conducting air strikes.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials cited by the Financial Times said Moscow was seeking to increase pressure on Kyiv and force it to accept Russian demands, including the ceding of territory in the Donbas, by early 2027.

articles.title: U.S. Withdraws All B-1B Strategic Bombers from RAF Fairford
articles.body:
The United States has withdrawn all B-1B strategic bombers deployed at the British RAF Fairford airfield.
The Pentagon and U.S. European Command (EUCOM) confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine the redeployment of the aircraft to their permanent bases in the United States.
On October 4, 12 B-1B Lancer bombers previously stationed in the United Kingdom left the air base throughout the day.
“We can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” the U.S. defense agency said in a statement to TWZ.
The Pentagon emphasized that the redeployment does not affect U.S. strategic bombers’ ability to conduct combat missions. B-1Bs, B-2s, and B-52s can carry out long-range combat missions directly from the continental United States.
The redeployment took place amid a counterterrorism investigation surrounding the airfield.
On September 27, British law enforcement received reports of three suspicious vehicles traveling toward RAF Fairford. Police detained five men aged between 23 and 25 near Welford. Police later released all five detainees on bail with restrictions, but they remain subjects of the investigation.
Britain’s Counter Terrorism Policing said they are investigating several possible lines of inquiry, including the possibility that the detainees may have been acting on behalf of a foreign state.
On September 30, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were indications of Iranian involvement in an alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack near RAF Fairford.
On October 1, police detained another man in London as part of the investigation. The British-Iranian national was suspected of preparing a terrorist attack. On October 3, he was released on bail, while the investigation remains ongoing.
However, as of now, British law enforcement has not publicly presented evidence conclusively establishing Iran’s involvement in the incident.
RAF Fairford plays an important role in U.S. strategic bomber operations in the Middle East. At the beginning of hostilities with Iran, the British government officially allowed the United States to use RAF Fairford for designated operations against Iranian missile forces.
The UK government said that U.S. operations from British bases were aimed at destroying Iranian missiles that posed a threat to allies and shipping. The first U.S. bomber deployed as part of this mission arrived at RAF Fairford in March 2026.
On July 22, the U.S. Air Force used B-1B Lancer to strike Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps facilities in Iran. The aircraft performed combat missions using the British RAF Fairford airfield.
On March 2, U.S. B-1Bs were used to strike ballistic missile production and storage facilities in Iran.
The scale of the U.S. deployment at RAF Fairford was so significant that organizers canceled the Royal International Air Tattoo 2026 air show in May.

articles.title: UK warships to enter South China Sea despite China protest
articles.body:
Royal Navy patrol ships HMS Spey and HMS Tamar are to enter the South China Sea for a ten-day multinational exercise with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore, continuing a British naval presence in waters where Beijing has repeatedly objected to UK military activity and policy, according to the Royal Navy.
The two Batch 2 River-class offshore patrol vessels will take part in Exercise Bersama Lima 26, the annual tri-service exercise conducted under the Five Power Defence Arrangements, or FPDA, which links the United Kingdom with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore.
Bersama Lima, meaning “Together Five” in Malay, will involve ships, aircraft and troops operating across maritime, land and air scenarios. Forces committed to the exercise include frigates, patrol vessels, a corvette, tanker and submarine, as well as divers and specialist boarding teams.
Australian F-35A Lightning II fighters will lead the air element of the exercise, while planned scenarios include troops directing naval gunfire, boarding and searching vessels at sea, anti-submarine warfare and naval air defence supported by participating air forces.
The deployment takes place against a long-running dispute between Beijing and several regional governments over territorial and maritime claims in the South China Sea, as well as wider disagreements over the activities of military forces from countries outside the region. China has repeatedly criticised British involvement. In 2018, Beijing said it had lodged stern representations with the UK after HMS Albion sailed close to the Paracel Islands, which China calls the Xisha Islands. China said the ship had entered waters it regarded as its territorial sea without permission, while Britain has consistently maintained the importance of navigational rights under international law.
Beijing again objected in 2021 as the UK increased its naval presence in the Indo-Pacific, accusing Britain of deploying its Carrier Strike Group to the South China Sea to “flex its naval muscles”. More recently, in July 2026, the Chinese Embassy in London strongly condemned the UK for joining an international statement supporting the 2016 South China Sea arbitration award and urged Britain to stop what it described as “stirring up trouble” in the region.
HMS Tamar has also recently conducted a freedom-of-navigation activity in the South China Sea. In a parliamentary answer published on 8 September, the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the patrol ship operated alongside the Royal Australian Navy on 1 September as part of the UK’s stated commitment to freedom of navigation and overflight under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The Royal Navy says HMS Spey and HMS Tamar have themselves conducted freedom-of-navigation missions in disputed waters during their five-year deployment to the Indo-Pacific, sometimes operating independently and sometimes alongside regional partners.
Before Bersama Lima moves into its main operational phase, personnel from the five participating nations will spend time familiarising themselves with different vessels, equipment, procedures and terminology, while senior officers carry out planning for the live exercise.
According to a Royal Navy news update, Lieutenant Commander Cheryl Goodwin, HMS Tamar’s Executive Officer, said: “We’re looking forward to being a part of Bersama Lima 26 – an exercise which unites some of our closest allies, tests the crew in a traditional war-fighting role, and demonstrates the UK’s resolve to maintain stability in the Indo-Pacific region through supporting our partners.”
HMS Tamar is also carrying a Royal New Zealand Navy boarding team during the exercise, adding another element of direct integration between the participating forces.
Lieutenant Williams, a Royal New Zealand Navy officer embarked aboard Tamar, said: “It’s a first for me and my team, but it’s a well-trodden path which has been established through a deep history of our navies working together.”
He added: “We’ve got a lot of experience to share, are always looking to improve and we’re ready to go.”
The Five Power Defence Arrangements were established in 1971 and provide a framework for defence cooperation between the five member states. Regular exercises bring together naval, land and air forces, particularly around Malaysia and Singapore, to practise combined operations and develop common procedures. Both British patrol ships have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021. Their mission, known as Operation Highwall, has included multinational exercises, maritime security operations, sanctions enforcement, humanitarian assistance, defence engagement and freedom-of-navigation activity.
Bersama Lima marks a return to operations for HMS Spey after the vessel spent the summer undergoing maintenance in Singapore. HMS Tamar has remained active across the region, including participation in the US-led Pacific Partnership humanitarian exercise and a visit to Cambodia before its September activity with the Royal Australian Navy in the South China Sea.
The ships passed five years continuously deployed to the Indo-Pacific in September, making them the first Royal Navy vessels to maintain a persistent presence in the region since the handover of Hong Kong in 1997.
During Bersama Lima, Spey and Tamar will operate as part of a larger multinational force, with the live phase testing the five FPDA nations across areas including maritime interdiction, anti-submarine warfare and air defence in and around the South China Sea.

articles.title: India Pushing for Bigger Role in Russia-Ukraine Talks
articles.body:
India is seeking a greater role in brokering an end to the Russia-Ukraine war, Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said on Sunday, as New Delhi steps up contacts with both sides.
“Our position on that conflict has been very clear, which is that we’d like to see an end to this conflict, and we believe that this will require dialogue and diplomacy,” Jaishankar said at a Munich Security Conference in New Delhi.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We have been advocating it for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy, so we have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard.”
Jaishankar said India was “trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping.”
But he said India was also “going beyond that,” including discussion on grain and energy exports and “on non-attack possibilities,” he said.
“Those are ongoing conversations right now,” he added.
Jaishankar made his first solo trip to Ukraine in September.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin have close ties, and the pair met in New Delhi in September.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that the United States wants to broker a new round of talks with Ukraine and Russia on ending the four-and-a-half-year war, aiming to hold them by the end of October.
The US-led peace efforts have been largely stalled with Washington’s attention shifted to its war with Iran and as Ukraine says Russia has ramped up its aerial attacks across the war-torn country.
Ukraine to Deploy Small Missiles, Turrets Against Jet Drones, Zelensky Says
Previous rounds of talks have failed to yield tangible progress towards peace, with Moscow unwilling to drop its maximalist conditions to end the fighting.

articles.title: US to send additional forces to Israel for potential escalation as both countries elections near
articles.body:
The US military has been conducting routine troop rotations in recent weeks, and additional troops and aircraft are expected to arrive in the coming weeks as part of preparations for an escalation in the Middle East, security sources told Walla on Sunday.
Some 3,000 US troops are currently stationed across Israel. Their duties include operating air defense systems, serving as pilots and support crews, and handling logistics and headquarters operations.
The Jerusalem Post previously reported that the Trump administration decided to deploy a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East, along with a second Marine division ahead of the US midterm elections.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt and an additional division of US Marines are currently en route to the Middle East for an extended deployment. The Roosevelt departed from San Francisco last Sunday.
A day later, the USS Makin Island amphibious ready group also departed San Diego, carrying the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit. The force includes about 2,200 Marines and personnel in the expeditionary unit, along with about 2,000 sailors aboard the group's three ships.
Israel's enemies watching Israeli, US elections
A senior Israeli defense official told Walla that Israel’s enemies are watching the elections in Israel and the US and considering whether and how to influence them through terrorist attacks. Such attacks would aim to unsettle the countries’ political systems without triggering a broader escalation.
“They understand that the Israeli response this time will be very aggressive.”
Iran is assessing whether the US is prepared to launch a military campaign against it and is conducting negotiations accordingly. Meanwhile, conditions in Iran are deteriorating on several fronts, particularly the economy. This comes as the US has succeeded in imposing conditions under which oil tankers are departing at nearly prewar levels.
Saudi Arabia, UAE ties to confront Houthis to have larger regional consequences
IDF officials say the campaign against the Houthis presents an opportunity to advance regional initiatives. Much depends on Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates strengthening ties and reaching agreements to confront their shared enemy, the Houthis.
According to senior IDF officials, such cooperation could encourage investment in Lebanon to displace Iranian investment and influence exercised through Hezbollah. It could also help build an anti-Iranian coalition in preparation for another military campaign.
A senior security official told Walla that there is an understanding that anyone who does not join the campaign against the Houthis now will be left alone and “will take hits from them accordingly.”
Preparing for another confrontation with Iran
The IDF is preparing for hostilities with Iran to erupt and escalate rapidly as Tehran struggles to cope with US sanctions and mounting economic pressure.
The military’s main focus is on the operations it would need to carry out if forced to launch extensive strikes against Iran, including identifying targets that would affect the extremist regime in Tehran.
Meanwhile, the IDF continues to coordinate closely with US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, in case Iran attempts to launch surprise missile barrages against Jordan and Israel.
Amichai Stein and Idan Kweller contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Robotic Turrets Record First Shootdowns of Russia’s Jet-Powered Geran-5 Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Robotic Turrets Record First Shootdowns of Russia’s Jet-Powered Geran-5 Drones
Ukraine has recorded its first confirmed interceptions of Russian jet-powered drones using automated gun turrets equipped with artificial intelligence and machine-vision systems, according to Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on October 5 that Ukraine’s robotic turret systems have already downed jet-powered UAVs, including Russia’s Geran-5. “There have already been shootdowns of even jet-powered UAVs, even the Geran-5, using those same turrets,” Ihnat said during Ukraine’s national telethon.
He said the systems rely on machine vision and artificial intelligence to automate targeting and reduce the role of human error during interception.
“The use of innovative technologies—artificial intelligence—eliminated human error. Machine vision is used specifically in the interception. Artificial intelligence makes it possible to engage even jet-powered UAVs,” Ihnat said.
The turrets have a relatively limited engagement range because their primary weapon remains a machine gun, according to Ihnat.
Russia has increasingly combined conventional Shahed-type attack drones with faster jet-powered UAVs during strikes against Ukraine. Ihnat said Russian forces launched around 50 jet-powered drones per night during each of the previous two nights.
According to figures cited by Ihnat, Ukrainian forces currently intercept approximately 85% to 92% of conventional Shahed-type drones. The estimated interception rate for jet-powered UAVs is lower, at around 50% to 70%.
The automated turrets are being deployed at selected locations, including around bridges, as Ukraine expands a layered defense network intended to protect infrastructure from low-flying attack drones.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 4 that more than 12 such turrets had already been deployed in Kyiv, with another eight planned for the surrounding Kyiv region.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine needs a combination of different air-defense systems as Russia adjusts its strike tactics and increasingly introduces faster drones and ballistic missiles alongside conventional Shahed-type UAVs.

articles.title: Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds: a small new missile named Nika, heading into testing
articles.body:
Ukraine has developed a new missile to knock down Russia's fast, jet-powered Shahed drones, the ones its air defenses catch far less often than older models, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 4 October, Suspilne reported. The weapon, called Nika, has not yet been tested. He announced it during a visit to Kyiv by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Russia's plants turn out an estimated 3,000 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, Ukraine's military intelligence estimates, and the jets fly fast enough to outrun the cheap interceptors built for slower, propeller-driven Shaheds. Ukraine plans about 400 units of just one of five interceptor models it is testing by the end of October, as it scrambles to close the gap before winter.
A new missile heads into testing
Both the Ukrainian and German sides have reacted positively to the missile, Zelenskyy said, though he stayed cautious on the result: for now, he said, it only "could be positive." In the same remarks, he announced a successful test of a separate system, the German-Ukrainian interceptor Spys.
Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges
Ukraine shoots down 85-92% of propeller-driven Shaheds, Zelenskyy said. Against the jet-powered variants, interception falls to roughly 50-60%, he noted at the press conference with Merz. F-16 fighter jets help close the gap, he said.
From interceptor drones to a new missile
Over the past month, Ukraine tested a new generation of drone interceptors built for the jet-Shahed threat. On 15 September, one struck a Shahed in trials, though Zelenskyy said developers still needed to refine its control system. On 19 September, he said the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) had created its own interceptor drone and used it to down a jet Shahed in combat. Nika adds a purpose-built missile to that mix.

articles.title: Officers involved in strikes on Ukraine were among eight killed in Tu-95MS crash in Russia
articles.body:
Officers involved in strikes on Ukraine were among eight killed in Tu-95MS crash in Russia
Eight military personnel were killed when a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in Russia's Amur Oblast on 29 September. At least three of them were officers involved in combat missions or their preparation, according to the Book of Executioners, a Ukrainian project documenting Russian war criminals and people who betrayed Ukraine.
Source: Russian media outlets Mediazona and The Insider
Details: Russian media outlets reported that the names of those killed had been posted in the Selskiye Novosti (Rural News) social media group for Seryshevo, a settlement near the Ukrainka strategic air base. OSINT analyst duke garland was the first to flag the post.
A photo featuring the portraits of the eight men killed was also released by Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky district in Amur Oblast. He said the local authorities would ask the long-range aviation command to put the crew forward for state awards.
Mediazona verified the list and confirmed that all eight served in Russia's strategic aviation.
According to the media outlets, those killed are:
- Andrei Lobanov, 40
- Vladislav Moskovskikh, 31
- Artur Yenokian, 30
- Mikhail Kotyshev, 23
- Sergei, 47, whose surname is reported as Monsevich by Mediazona and Moisevich by The Insider
- Vladimir Kelip, 55
- Fedor Pavlyukov, 43
- Andrei Gerasimov, 36.
The OSINT analyst believes the portraits in the announcement follow the standard order in which Tu-95MS crew members are listed. On that basis, Lobanov was the crew commander, Moskovskikh the co-pilot, Yenokian the navigator, Kotyshev the navigator-operator (responsible for operating the bomber's mission systems), Monsevich the flight engineer, and Kelip the radio operator. Pavlyukov and Gerasimov were likely passengers or inspectors.
Mediazona says the quality of the photograph makes it difficult to establish the military ranks of all those killed with certainty.
The Insider checked the names against the Ukrainian Book of Executioners database and found Lobanov, Pavlyukov and Gerasimov in its records. Details about them had been added before the plane crashed.
As of November 2025, Major Andrei Lobanov was listed in the database as the deputy commander of a Tu-95MS squadron of the 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, based at the Ukrainka airfield. According to the project, he directly commanded the unit and personally participated in combat missions.
Lieutenant Colonel Fedor Pavlyukov is listed as the regiment's deputy commander for flight training. He commanded a Tu-95MS squadron from August 2021 to April 2024. According to the project, he was responsible for preparing flight personnel for combat missions and directly led the unit.
Furthermore, in March 2022, Ukrainian intelligence included Pavlyukov on a list of Russian long-range aviation pilots who, according to its data, were being prepared to participate in the war against Ukraine.
Andrei Gerasimov is listed in the Book of Executioners as a major and commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment. According to the database, he commanded the unit and personally took part in combat missions. However, Mediazona's casualty list gives his rank as lieutenant colonel.
Ukrainian serviceman and blogger Anatolii Shtefan also reported that at least three of those killed were involved in organising and executing missile strikes on Ukraine. Shtefan did not specify whom exactly he was referring to.
According to Port Amur, cited by The Insider, there were nine military personnel on board. The bodies of two of the crew members were not found immediately. The Russian Ministry of Defence initially reported six dead and one taken to hospital.
Background:
- On 29 September, the Tu-95MS crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo in the Mazanovsky district in Amur Oblast.
- The Russian Defence Ministry claimed that the bomber was conducting a training flight without ammunition when it crashed in an unpopulated area. Regional authorities said the crew steered the aircraft away from residential buildings, and no one on the ground was injured.
- The Russian Defence Ministry sent an Aerospace Forces commission to the site to establish what caused the crash. Kommersant reported that investigators had tentatively attributed it to a technical malfunction. The Insider notes, however, that no conclusions about the cause of the crash have been publicly confirmed.
- According to Mediazona, most of those killed had served at the Engels strategic bomber airbase in Saratov Oblast before moving to the Ukrainka airbase. According to the outlet, Russia began pulling its strategic bombers out of Engels after Ukraine launched its first drone attacks on the airfield.
- After the Security Service of Ukraine carried out Operation Spider's Web, the Ukrainka airbase in Russia's Far East became one of the main bases for its strategic aviation. According to The Insider, a Tu-95MS combat mission from the base, involving stopovers at Engels or Olenya airfield, missile launches and the return flight, can cover more than 12,000 km and last around 23 hours. The outlet notes that flights of this length accelerate wear on the aircraft and their engines, shortening their service life.

articles.title: Jet-Powered Interceptor Likely Developed Based on Bars Missile-Drone
articles.body:
A jet-powered interceptor was likely developed based on the Bars missile-drone. It is currently demonstrating the highest effectiveness against Russian drones.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this during a joint news conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv.
“Second, interceptor drones. The Bars have shown positive results. They currently have the highest percentage. Others are also catching up. God willing, there will be competition in the good sense of the word,” he said.
Although it is probably impossible to determine whether Zelensky was referring specifically to an adaptation of Bars missile-drones or to a jet-powered interceptor with the same name, a number of factors support the adaptation theory. Ukraine and Germany already have an agreement on the joint production of these missile-drones.
In addition, RBC-Ukraine previously reported, citing its own sources in military circles, that Ukrainian jet-powered drone platforms currently used for long-range strikes were being adapted. According to the publication’s sources, “some solutions based on them have already demonstrated good results in the role of interceptors.”
According to the president, the Bars jet-powered interceptor currently has an interception rate of about 30% against aerial targets.
The president also spoke separately about agreements with Germany on the production of interceptor drones. According to him, Ukraine is to receive 2,000 Bars drones, which will be manufactured as part of joint production. Funding for the program has already been provided by the German side.
Overall, according to the president, the Defense Forces intercept about 50-55% of Russian jet-powered drones, and “sometimes 60%,” while the rate for conventional Shahed drones is 85-92%, depending on the composition of the Russian attack.
It was previously reported that the main obstacles to the production of jet-powered interceptor drones are a shortage of engines and limited budget funding.
“Engines are a key element; we really import them in large quantities. There are also domestically produced engines, but there are not enough of them,” Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times.
The Bars has been under development since 2023, but its first photos appeared only recently. During that time, its design underwent more than 40 engineering upgrades.
The platform currently has several variants: some modifications have a range of up to 1,000 kilometers, a payload of up to 60 kilograms, and a speed exceeding 700 km/h.
According to the stated specifications, the Bars is a modular platform that allows the aircraft to be rapidly adapted to specific missions. Its modularity enables three main categories of use: DeepStrike, MiddleStrike and FrontStrike.
Changing the configuration allows the balance between fuel tank volume and warhead weight to be adjusted to create different modifications.
“We use the capabilities provided by AI technologies today and are not afraid to apply them at all levels — from development and solving engineering tasks to implementing machine vision in our target-guidance systems,” the developer said.

articles.title: 163 combat clashes at front in past day, most in Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka directions – General Staff
articles.body:
Russian troops have attacked the positions of the Defense Forces of Ukraine 163 times since the beginning of the day, with the enemy being most active in Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports.
"In total, 163 combat clashes have occurred since the beginning of this day. Russia launched 1 missile strike and 54 airstrikes, dropping 158 guided aerial bombs. In addition, it deployed 5,226 kamikaze drones for strikes and carried out 1,641 shellings of settlements and the positions of our troops," the report states.
In North Slobozhanske and Kursk directions, the Defense Forces repelled one Russian assault action. Russia launched four airstrikes using 13 guided aerial bombs and carried out 132 shellings of Ukrainian troop positions and settlements, 13 of which were with the use of multiple launch rocket systems (MLRS).
Throughout the day in South Slobozhanske direction, Russia assaulted the positions of Ukrainian units four times – near Lyman and toward the settlements of Ternova and Zakharivka; two combat clashes are ongoing.
In Kupiansk direction, the Defense Forces repelled one Russian attack in the area of Kupiansk-Vuzlovy.
In Lyman direction, Ukrainian defenders repelled six attempts by Russians to advance near the settlements of Derylove, Drobysheve, Zarichne, and Lyman; another combat clash is ongoing.
In Sloviansk direction, the Defense Forces stopped one attempt by the invaders to move forward in the area of Mykolaivka.
One Russian assault was recorded in the Kramatorsk direction near the settlement of Fedorivka Druha.
In Kostiantynivka direction, the Defense Forces repelled 22 Russian assaults in the areas of Kostiantynivka and Novoselivka, and in the direction of Osykove, Mykolaipillia, Raiske, and Torske.
A total of 21 attacks were repelled in Pokrovsk direction. Russia tried to advance in the areas of Bilytske, Svitle, Vasylivka, Molodetske, and in the direction of Hannivka, Dobropillia, and Serhiivka.
"According to preliminary estimates, 71 occupiers were eliminated and 26 wounded here today; seven units of automotive equipment, one multiple launch rocket system, seven units of special equipment, one unmanned aerial vehicle control post, two fuel and lubricant depots, and 27 enemy shelters were destroyed. One tank, 11 units of automotive equipment, three multiple launch rocket systems, two electronic warfare devices, four guns, three units of special equipment, seven unmanned aerial vehicle control posts, and 182 Russian shelters were damaged. 292 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed," the report says.
Ukrainian defenders repelled one occupier attack in Oleksandrivka direction near Novoheorhiivka.
Two Russian attacks were recorded in Huliaipole direction, in the area of Huliaipole and toward the settlement of Kopani.
In Orikhiv direction, the Defense Forces repelled two Russian attacks in the area of Mala Tokmachka and toward Novoiakovlivka.

articles.title: Ukraine has largely exhausted its air defense capabilities — military analyst
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 5. /TASS/. The capabilities of Ukraine’s air defense forces have largely been exhausted, and the Ukrainian armed forces are unable to repel strikes by the Russian Armed Forces, military analyst Igor Korotchenko, editor-in-chief of the National Defense magazine, told TASS.
"To a large extent, the capabilities of Ukraine’s existing air defense forces have been exhausted. But this does not mean that there is no air defense at all. Our capabilities are now much more effective due to the use of new weapons systems, so Ukraine’s existing air defense forces cannot fully counter our strikes, and they are unable to intercept ballistic missiles at all, since they do not yet have the appropriate capabilities," said the military analyst.
He noted that Russia has modernized its Geran family of drones. The new versions feature higher speed and enable high-precision strikes in the final stage of the flight path. According to the military analyst, the enemy currently has no means of intercepting them in the airspace.

articles.title: Geran-5 Gets Kh-101-Like Guidance as Russia Pushes Its Jet Drones Toward Full Autonomy
articles.body:

Geran-5 Gets Kh-101-Like Guidance as Russia Pushes Its Jet Drones Toward Full Autonomy
Russia has equipped its newer jet-powered Geran drones with an electro-optical navigation system that lets them autonomously fly toward targets by comparing camera imagery with a stored visual map of the route, bringing their guidance concept closer to that used on some Kh-101 cruise missiles, Defense Express reported on October 5.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence recently released new details on the Geran-5 K5 and a newer Geran-4 variant that Russian forces began using this fall. Both reportedly carry a system known as Susannin, designed to reduce the drone’s dependence on an external control signal during the flight.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Rather than relying on an operator continuously steering the aircraft through a communications network, Susannin uses onboard imagery. The drone compares what its camera sees below with reference images loaded into the system and uses those visual matches to determine where it is and continue along its programmed route.
In practical terms, the aircraft can navigate by “looking” at the terrain. Defense Express notes that this means mesh modems and airborne mesh repeaters are not necessarily required for the drone to reach its intended target, since the navigation process can continue autonomously without a constant outside command link.
A similar principle has already appeared in more sophisticated Russian long-range weapons. One version of the air-launched Kh-101 cruise missile, known as Izdeliye 504AP, used an optical navigation system called Otblesk-U during Russian missile strikes against Ukraine between 2022 and 2025.
That comparison is important because it shows Russia gradually transferring technologies associated with expensive cruise missiles into cheaper unmanned strike systems. The goal appears to be making jet-powered Geran drones increasingly independent, accurate, and less reliant on vulnerable communications links during their approach to a target.
The change also comes as Ukraine becomes more effective at intercepting Russia’s newer jet-powered UAVs. Defense Express estimates that Ukrainian forces are already destroying roughly 50% to 60% of them, meaning that only around four or five out of every 10 launched may currently reach their targets.
Improving autonomous navigation could therefore be part of Russia’s effort to increase the number of drones that survive long enough to complete their missions, particularly as Ukraine expands dedicated interceptor-drone units and other counter-UAV defenses.
The Geran-5 and newer Geran-4 are part of a broader Russian effort to move beyond the original propeller-driven Shahed concept. Their jet propulsion already gives them significantly greater speed, while systems such as Susannin add another layer of sophistication by allowing the aircraft to navigate visually without depending on continuous external guidance.
The result is a weapon that increasingly sits somewhere between a conventional one-way strike drone and a small cruise missile: cheaper and simpler than weapons such as the Kh-101, but borrowing some of the same ideas in navigation and terminal autonomy.
Earlier, a Geran-type drone equipped with a turbojet engine entered Moldovan airspace and later crashed and exploded near a road in the Orhei district on the evening of September 30.

articles.title: German intelligence head warns of threat of violent conflict with Russia

German intelligence head warns of threat of violent conflict with Russia
Martin Jäger, head of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service, has stated that he sees the danger of a violent conflict with Russia, noting that the confrontation between the countries has acquired a "new, dangerous quality".
Source: European Pravda, citing Jäger's remarks during a hearing in the Bundestag, quoted by Die Welt
Details: The German intelligence head warned that the war in Ukraine, marked by increasingly brutal Russian attacks, is entering a "new, very dangerous phase", while the threat of hybrid attacks against Germany remains real.
Jäger stated that the risk involves Germany being dragged into a conflict with Russia.
The intelligence head emphasised that Russia is visibly escalating the conflict in Ukraine and continues to step up pressure on Europe and Germany. The confrontation Germany is in with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous character. The country risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia.
As an example of this escalation, he cited the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, responsibility for which Berlin attributed to Russia.
Jäger noted that no other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany. Germany did not seek this confrontation. Russia is imposing it on the country, seeing it as its main adversary because Germany does not tolerate Russia's revisionist, expansionist policy and its war of aggression against Ukraine.
According to Jäger, the Russian leadership seeks to "ensure for the future that no political decisions directed against Moscow are made in Berlin or other European capitals". The consequence of this is "increasingly aggressive actions by Russian intelligence services" against Germany and other states.
Jäger stated that Russia is waging a shadow war against Germany. This undeclared war cannot be characterised using traditional military or legal categories. Germany is not in a state of defence, yet they are still under attack – that is precisely what a shadow war is.
The intelligence head added that Russia sought to undermine Europe's political support for Ukraine and emphasised that they had to be prepared for intimidation attempts and further interference. He noted that nuclear threats would likely be voiced again.
However, according to Jäger, at this time the intelligence agency sees no signs of a large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory. Nevertheless, "Russian military actions on a limited scale" are possible, particularly in the Baltic states, specified the head of German intelligence.
