articles.title: Brazilians head to polls in pivotal election
articles.body:
Polls close in Brazil’s pivotal election
The polls have closed in Brazil’s hotly contested presidential election, which could reshape the country’s domestic and foreign policy.
The race is dominated by incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing challenger, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Lula is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term in office. More than a dozen other candidates are also on the ballot.
Polls released on the eve of the election showed Lula and Bolsonaro neck and neck. Quaest put them at 46% and 45%, respectively, while Datafolha had Lula at 45% and Bolsonaro at 42%, with both surveys showing a statistical tie. If neither candidate wins more than half of the vote, a runoff will be held on October 25. All other candidates are polling in the low single digits, but their endorsements could prove important in a second round.
Brazilians will also elect all 513 federal congress members, 54 of the country’s 81 senators, 27 governors, and some regional legislatures.
Lula campaigned on his left-leaning Workers’ Party platform, promising continued welfare programs, state-funded development, and income redistribution. He framed the vote as a choice between “strengthening democracy and barbarism.”
Bolsonaro called for change, blaming Lula’s policies for high living costs and promising tougher security policies and tax cuts. The 45-year-old senator for Rio de Janeiro has also leaned heavily on the image of his father, known to supporters as ‘mito’ (the legend).
Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was sentenced to 27 years behind bars for attempting to overturn the results of the 2022 presidential election, which he lost to Lula. He has denied wrongdoing. He spent several months in prison after breaking house arrest monitoring rules before being hospitalized in March 2026 over health issues and eventually transferred back to temporary house arrest, which has since been extended.
Why does this election matter?
Brazil is a founding member of BRICS and has played a prominent role in the group. Under Lula, Brasilia has pursued a policy focused on strengthening multipolarity and resisting Western pressure, particularly from Washington.
The Trump administration has placed renewed emphasis on US dominance in the Western Hemisphere under what it calls the ‘Donroe Doctrine’, a modern interpretation of the 19th-century hegemonic political strategy known as the Monroe Doctrine.
Washington has said it intends to strengthen US influence across the Americas while preventing rival powers, particularly China, from gaining strategic footholds there.
Opposing ‘colonization’
During his current term, Lula has criticized the US over what he described as attempts to undermine multipolarity and impose its will on other nations.
Last year, India and Brazil stepped up talks on trade and investment after both countries were hit with 50% tariffs by the US. Lula also called for a coordinated BRICS response to Washington’s tariff policies, accusing Trump of attempts to “dismantle multilateralism” and promote “unilateralism, where he negotiates one-on-one with other countries.”
The Brazilian president also sharply condemned the US kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in early 2026. In March, he proposed boosting defense cooperation with South Africa to reduce reliance on foreign weapons, arguing that both nations could be vulnerable to “invasion.”
In late September, he openly accused Trump of seeking to “colonize” Brazil and gain control of its natural resources. “What Trump wants is to colonize Brazil, to take our wealth, steal our future and leave us behind,” he said at the time.
‘Trump’s candidate’?
Flavio Bolsonaro, who Lula has described as “Trump’s candidate,” has emphasized his affinity with the US president and repeatedly praised him, while denying receiving assistance from Washington for his campaign. He has insisted that Brazil should seek better deals with the US, including rare-earth minerals – a topic that has been repeatedly invoked by US President Donald Trump in his talks with various nations, including Ukraine and Russia.
The senator also promised a “flood of investments” from the US if he wins. “Brazil and the United States will once again have a high-level and long-term relationship, including the largest trade and investment agreement in our history!” Bolsonaro wrote in a post on X in June.
He has also vowed to “truly combat Brazilian terrorist organizations and restore sovereignty to more than 50 million Brazilians who live in areas dominated by them,” without specifying which groups he meant.
Bolsonaro has also reportedly pledged to join the US campaign against drug cartels. The US military has at times targeted boats supposedly belonging to traffickers, killing dozens of people.
Shadow of interference
The Brazilian authorities have opened a probe into allegations that the US government funded activities aimed at interfering in the election and undermining the legitimacy of the country’s Supreme Federal Court, Agencia Brasil reported on Friday.
This followed a report by The Guardian earlier in the week, claiming that the White House planned to allocate $1 million for a project titled ‘Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil’.
US social media giant Meta also blocked the advertising account on Facebook used by Lula’s campaign, preventing it from running new ads just days before the first round. The account was restored later the same day, with Meta providing no immediate explanation.
In September, Lula cited a confidential assessment by the Brazilian Intelligence Agency, which warned that the risk of US interference in the election was at a “critical level.”
Trump avoided openly endorsing any candidates ahead of the election, but said he was following it “very closely.”
“Brazil is a very important country. The people of Brazil are fantastic. These are very important elections,” he said on Thursday.
Moscow has expressed hope that the election would be held “without any adverse external interference.”
“We are open to… continuing our cooperation with our Brazilian partners across the entire agenda,” the head of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Latin American Department, Aleksandr Shetinin, told TASS.

articles.title: Don’t know? Blame Russia: Finnish president takes page from NATO chief’s playbook
articles.body:
Don’t know? Blame Russia: Finnish president takes page from NATO chief’s playbook
Published 5 Oct, 2026 04:09 | Updated 5 Oct, 2026 09:27
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has blamed Russia for a wide range of security concerns facing the EU, including the influx of migrants over the summer into Ceuta, Spain’s enclave in Morocco. He later admitted that he did not know the situation in Ceuta “well enough to take a position.”
Stubb made the remarks in an interview with Spanish newspaper El Mundo over the weekend. Asked about potential hybrid threats posed by Russia, Stubb said the country would try to interfere with the upcoming Spanish election.
Madrid “should expect some form of sabotage or hybrid attack. It could be related to information warfare or a campaign that threatens their democracy,” he claimed.
The president went on to allege that Russian-backed cyberattacks are “happening as we speak against Spanish banks and other targets,” without citing specific evidence.
“They send asylum seekers to our border, as we have also seen in Ceuta,” he said, accusing Russia of committing acts of sabotage throughout the EU.
He also mentioned cases in which Russian-linked ships were accused of cutting undersea telecommunications cables in the Baltic Sea and the recent incident at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport, where explosives-laden drones were found near Ukrainian cargo planes. Germany blamed Moscow and ordered the closure of a Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural center in Berlin. Russia dismissed the accusations as “nonsensical” and denied any involvement.
Pressed further about Russia’s alleged role in the Ceuta crisis in late July, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the enclave, Stubb admitted that he did not “know the matter well enough to take a position.”
Reuters reported at the time that migrants had been encouraged by viral videos and misleading claims about Spain’s asylum and migration rules. Spain later accused Russian- and Israeli-linked networks of spreading disinformation regarding the crisis, which both countries denied.
Stubb’s interview came after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte encouraged members of the bloc to attribute incidents to Russia whenever they are sure or “almost sure” that Russia is responsible.
“When able, when you are sure it is the Russians, or almost sure it is the Russians, attribute it to the Russians,” Rutte said this week.
Direct conflict unlikely
Asked about the possibility of a direct conflict between NATO and Russia, however, Stubb dismissed it as negligible.
“Do we expect Russia to attack? The answer is no. We have no evidence of that,” he told El Mundo.
According to the Finnish president, EU leaders have a “communication problem,” as some have been “acting in an alarmist way and conflating [hypothetical] scenarios with the perception of the threat.”
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius urged officials this week not to “exaggerate” when making alarmist statements about Russia and said there is no evidence that the country is planning to attack NATO. Rutte has also said there is “no imminent threat to NATO territory.”
Nevertheless, EU officials have argued that the bloc, as well as NATO, should be prepared for a potential clash with Russia. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the country must be ready for a conflict by as early as 2028. The German government amended its constitutional debt brake to fund military spending and passed a 2026 budget allocating a record €108.2 billion ($121.5 billion) to defense and €11.5 billion in military assistance for Ukraine.
Russia has stated that it would not attack any NATO country unless attacked first – warning, however, that Western military aid to Ukraine makes a dangerous escalation more likely. President Vladimir Putin has argued that European politicians are stirring tensions with Russia to distract voters from problems at home.

Today, the Americans are announcing many competitions, analyzing the industry, including ours, and also adopting Ukrainian experience from the war against the Russian Federation

As one example, he cited the creation of a marketplace through which military formations can directly purchase products from registered manufacturers. According to Pinchuk, the Americans are using Ukrainian developments in some such solutions.
Ukrainian defense companies are simultaneously entering the American market with increasing activity. In particular, the U.S. company UDD, created by the Ukrainian company F-Drones, won the first stage of the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program and received a contract to supply 2,000 drones.

It is intended to directly bring together military personnel and weapons manufacturers from both countries to find responses to new technological threats.
At the same time, a full-fledged exchange of technologies still faces obstacles. According to Pinchuk, Ukraine lacks a specialized structure responsible for the security of defense technology transfers and capable of guaranteeing partners the protection of transferred developments.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia explored new routes oil export amid Hormuz crisis
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Aramco eyes new oil routes to bypass Strait of Hormuz
Saudi Arabia's Aramco is examining proposals for two new land-based oil export routes that would bypass the Strait of Hormuz, as continued military tensions disrupt shipping, tankers come under attack and freight rates soar.
According to a report published on 27 September by BN Report, a platform specialising in energy intelligence and business economics, the Saudi oil giant is conducting engineering and technical feasibility studies to expand its export routes.
The proposals include connecting pipelines to Oman's coast and the Duqm storage complex, giving Saudi Arabia direct access to Asian markets while reducing its exposure to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and rising insurance premiums.
US-based Business Insurance magazine, which specialises in risk and insurance intelligence, reported on 1 October that war-risk insurance premiums for Saudi-linked tankers had tripled to 3% of a vessel's value at Yanbu port. At southern ports, premiums had risen to 7%, adding millions of dollars to the cost of individual shipments.
The plans come as the Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi oil facilities, with the group announcing that it had carried out a "qualitative military operation" using several ballistic missiles and drones targeting Saudi Aramco in the capital Riyadh.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Saturday, 3 October, that the operation "comes as part of the response to Saudi Arabia's targeting" of the Yemeni capital Sanaa and other areas under the group's control.
The Houthis also said they would continue to impose the equation of "siege for siege and escalation for escalation".
Investment costs decline
Strategic, economic and infrastructure considerations are increasingly shaping the region's energy transport calculations, according to economic expert Hossam Ayesh.
Ayesh told The New Arab that the huge investment costs and lengthy construction periods involved in building new pipelines must be weighed against rising insurance premiums and the risks facing maritime shipping.
Although shipping oil by sea may theoretically remain cheaper than constructing thousands of kilometres of pipelines, geopolitical tensions and the risk of the Strait of Hormuz being closed are pushing policymakers to look beyond traditional export routes, he said.
These calculations also come amid shifts in international competition.
Bloomberg reported on 29 September that the vulnerability of logistical hubs in the Middle East coincides with rising production in the Americas, which is expected to exceed 32 million barrels per day by 2030. This puts further pressure on Gulf producers to secure reliable export routes and protect their market share in Asia as alternative supplies grow.
Gulf states are also drawing lessons from recent disruptions to international energy infrastructure, particularly the fallout from the Nord Stream pipelines linking Russia and Germany.
The pipelines were sabotaged and subsequently halted amid the war in Ukraine, causing major financial losses.
The precedent shows that new pipelines would not be immune to targeting or sabotage, particularly amid heightened global uncertainty and sharp fluctuations in oil demand, Ayesh said.
Through the proposed routes, policymakers at Aramco and in Saudi Arabia are seeking to diversify oil export options through the Red Sea, domestic pipelines and potential land routes towards Oman, Jordan and Syria.
The aim is to safeguard vital market share and ensure reliable supplies despite mounting security threats, according to Ayesh.
This makes the financial cost a secondary consideration compared with the strategic need to ensure the sustainability and reliability of Saudi oil exports, he added.
The project could also go beyond transporting Saudi oil and play a role in strengthening logistical and economic integration with neighbouring countries, particularly Oman.
Its scope could eventually expand to include the transport of Qatari liquefied natural gas towards the Arabian Sea, according to Ayesh, who said shared infrastructure could generate additional economic benefits across the region.
Riyadh-Muscat partnership
Aramco's study of new export routes represents a major strategic investment aimed primarily at strengthening the security and resilience of Saudi oil exports and protecting them from future shocks, according to economic expert Ali Metwally, who works at a London-based consultancy.
Metwally told The New Arab that the project could be implemented in stages over several years, particularly if one of the routes includes a direct connection to Oman's Arabian Sea coast.
The estimated cost of building a major regional pipeline with a capacity of between 1.5 million and 2.5 million barrels per day ranges from $8 billion to $15 billion for a single route.
Costs could rise further with the addition of major pumping stations, storage facilities, maritime export terminals and advanced protection and operating systems.
Metwally stressed that the figures remain preliminary until Aramco announces official details on the project's approved capacity and final budget.
The case for alternative routes is being strengthened by continued disruption to seaborne oil flows.
Lloyd's List, a London-based maritime data and intelligence provider, reported on 2 October that congestion affecting ship-to-ship oil transfers in the Gulf of Oman was prompting tanker owners to bypass bottlenecks around the strait in favour of alternative ports.
The shift reflects growing expectations that the shipping crisis could persist for years.
The project's economic value lies partly in avoiding soaring insurance premiums and maritime shipping costs, which could rise to tens of dollars per barrel during periods of heightened tensions and clashes around the Strait of Hormuz.
Rather than comparing pipeline construction costs with ordinary shipping costs during periods of stability, Metwally argues that the pipeline's fixed capital costs would be spread across long-term contracts and millions of barrels transported each day, potentially making the project financially viable as maritime risks increase.
A route linking Saudi Arabia and Oman would also provide additional strategic value by giving Saudi oil direct access to major Asian markets without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, using Duqm port and other terminals on the Arabian Sea, according to Metwally.
It would draw on Oman's developed logistics infrastructure and large storage facilities, potentially creating deeper regional integration in oil handling, tanker shipping and strategic stock management.
Aramco's commercial gain
For Aramco, the main commercial benefit would be greater supply reliability for major importers and a reduced risk of losing its established market share in Asia to competing energy suppliers.
The proposed routes would create a more flexible export network, allowing the Saudi oil giant to redirect shipments between the Gulf, Red Sea and Arabian Sea depending on security risks, insurance costs and global demand, according to Metwally.
However, one of the biggest obstacles would be constructing a route stretching more than 1,000 kilometres across harsh desert environments, including the Empty Quarter.
This would pose significant technical challenges, including extreme temperatures and shifting dunes, as well as the need to establish electricity networks, maintenance infrastructure and secure access routes.
The project would also require Riyadh and Muscat to reach comprehensive bilateral agreements governing ownership and operating rights, tariffs and security arrangements.

articles.title: Ukraine touts gains from Operation Vivaldi as Russia claims major encirclements. What’s really happening on the battlefield?
articles.body:
Ukraine touts gains from Operation Vivaldi as Russia claims major encirclements. What’s really happening on the battlefield?
The Russian and Ukrainian armies continue their offensives in different sectors of the front. Because these operations have coincided with a new burst of activity in the negotiations mediated by Donald Trump, they have been accompanied by loud public relations campaigns. The Russian command describes its offensive as “destroying encircled groupings,” though in reality it has failed to encircle any major Ukrainian forces. Ukrainian military officials claim they have already moved on to the third phase of “Operation Vivaldi” near the city of Lyman in Donetsk region. Judging by open-source videos, however, they are still working — successfully — to push Russian forces off their first line of defense. In reality, the nature of the fighting has not changed. The Russian army is trying to break through to the Kramatorsk-Sloviansk urban area from different directions, while Ukrainian forces are trying to stop this advance with counterattacks. This battle is of decisive importance for the course of the war even without the additional public relations campaigns, which are more likely to mislead.
Vladimir Putin, speaking last week at a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, said “the authorities in Ukraine and Europe themselves believe they’ll be able to hold Donbas for only a year and a half to two years.” Russian forces, he said, will capture it “much sooner.” Putin assured the experts gathered at the event that the pace of the offensive is “accelerating.”
In reality, the Russian army captured Pokrovsk and Siversk by early 2026 and Kostiantynivka that summer, but over the following nine months failed to break through into the cities defending the Kramatorsk urban area from the south, northeast, and southwest. In the northeast, around Lyman, Russian forces lost much of the territory they had captured the previous year.
‘Operation Vivaldi’ and fighting on the Siverskyi Donets
- Andrii Biletskyi, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, who recently took charge of all forces defending Kramatorsk and Sloviansk from the north, east, and south (the newly formed “Center” grouping), said troops have begun the next phase of “Operation Vivaldi.” The goal of the operation — which, like the Italian composer’s famous work, is supposed to have four parts — remains unclear. Ukrainian forces are likely planning to push Russia’s 20th and 25th armies back across the Chornyi Zherebets, a tributary of the Siverskyi Donets. As a result, Russian forces risk losing all the gains they have made in this sector since the summer of 2025, when they crossed the Chornyi Zherebets along a broad front.
- Biletskyi has described the operation’s progress only in general terms, but many in Ukraine, unofficially, see it as something close to a harbinger of a new tactic that could help Ukrainian forces defeat the Russian army. The pace of “Vivaldi” so far shows no sign of such a shift: Ukrainian troops, who began the offensive in mid-summer, have advanced no more than 10 kilometers (6 miles) in different sectors.
- Videos that surfaced in recent weeks were meant to confirm Ukrainian successes. They show Ukrainian forces liberating several villages on the perimeter of the Russian salient around Lyman — Novoselivka, Shandryholove, and Nove — and attempting to gain a foothold in Serednie, Karpivka, and Katerynivka, villages that had been on the line of contact for months.
- Russia’s 20th Combined Arms Army, which faces Ukrainian forces in this sector, was previously thought to have largely withdrawn across the Chornyi Zherebets. Now, if the published videos mark the farthest extent of the Ukrainian advance, the 20th Army appears to still hold positions on the western bank of the Chornyi Zherebets near Zarichne and in the surrounding forests and ravines. The Russian position is worsening, however: Ukrainian assault troops have pushed deep into the flanks at Nove and Kolodiazi.
- To the south, meanwhile, Russia’s 25th Army continues to hold positions on the outskirts of Lyman. One video shows Russian assault troops back in the city center, which had largely been cleared of them earlier in the summer after a failed assault. Problems facing the neighboring 20th Army are worsening conditions on the 25th Army’s northern flank, and if Ukrainian forces capture the Chornyi Zherebets crossings at Torske and Zarichne, the 25th Army will have to withdraw from Lyman.
- The Russian offensive on Lyman was meant to support the 3rd Combined Arms Army’s advance along the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets toward Sloviansk. That plan worked until Russian forces were stopped near Lyman and on the approaches to Sviatohirsk, farther west. Problems facing its neighbors on the northern bank have recently forced the 3rd Army to fight its way toward Sloviansk alone. By late summer, its troops had reached the city of Mykolaivka, 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Sloviansk, but failed to take it in a quick assault, though Russian assault troops did reach its eastern outskirts.
- In recent weeks, Ukrainian forces have tried to eliminate the threat to Mykolaivka through counterattacks near Rai-Oleksandrivka, reaching the village center, where heavy fighting has broken out. Russian forces still control the southeastern approaches to Mykolaivka, though, and are trying to outflank the Ukrainian units advancing on Rai-Oleksandrivka near the Siverskyi Donets–Donbas canal in the Yurkivka and Orikhuvatka area.
- These battles will determine whether Russian forces get closer to Sloviansk’s outskirts in 2026. Biletskyi’s troops are likely to try a larger counterattack on the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets.
Dobropillia and Druzhkivka
- Russian forces are trying to go around the Kramatorsk urban area from the west. In their path is one of Ukraine’s “fortresses”: the city of Dobropillia. Russian troops spent the first half of the year covering the 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Pokrovsk, which they had already captured, to Dobropillia’s southern outskirts. Forces in this sector needed significant reinforcement: the 76th Airborne Assault Division was redeployed to the area from other sectors first, followed by the 90th Tank Division.
- In September, the Russian Defense Ministry unexpectedly announced that Dobropillia had been encircled. A month earlier, Putin had expressed displeasure with the slow pace of the advance to the commander of the 76th Division. Judging by that conversation and the place names mentioned in it, Russian forces were only about five kilometers (3 miles) from the city at the time and were not even contemplating an encirclement.
- In the two weeks since the encirclement announcement, no evidence has emerged that Dobropillia has been outflanked from the west or east. Ukrainian forces, judging by published videos, managed to regain control of Hannivka, the city’s northeastern outskirts. Russian assault troops did enter Dobropillia itself from the south, however, beginning an assault on the city.
- At the same time, Russian forces are widening the front of their offensive around Dobropillia. The 90th Tank Division and its neighbors advanced several kilometers north in the sector between Dobropillia and Druzhkivka, while units of the 2nd Combined Arms Army pushed southwest of the city in the Hrushynka River valley.
- Although Dobropillia isn’t encircled, the situation around it is growing increasingly difficult for Ukrainian forces. Russian forces, after redeploying large reserves, now hold a significant advantage in the area.
- In September, Biletskyi described Russia’s plan for the Donbas offensive this way: the Russian “northern pincer” was meant to cut supply routes to Kramatorsk and Sloviansk by crossing the Siverskyi Donets near Sviatohirsk and Lyman and blocking the roads to Izyum and Kharkiv, while the “southern pincer,” advancing through Dobropillia, was meant to cut the road out of Kramatorsk near Barvinkove and complete the encirclement of the Kramatorsk urban area. The “defeat of the northern pincer” near Lyman, Biletskyi said, eliminated that threat. Russia’s plan now appears far more modest, however: after capturing Dobropillia, Russian forces want to push directly along the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk road toward the center of the urban area, as well as from Chasiv Yar toward the heights south of Kramatorsk. Defending Dobropillia and the territory east of the city will require Ukraine’s military command to urgently redeploy additional forces.
The ‘Vovchansk encirclement’
- The Russian command has announced another “encirclement” far beyond the Donbas front. In May 2024, when Russia launched a new invasion of the Kharkiv region using forces of the Leningrad Military District (the “Sever” grouping), the Russian General Staff likely planned to combine this offensive with the assault on Donbas: after capturing Vovchansk, troops were supposed to push through Velykyi Burluk into the rear of Ukrainian forces defending Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. This mirrored the Russian operation in 2022, when Russian forces reached Izyum within the first days of the full-scale invasion, crossed the Siverskyi Donets after heavy fighting, and advanced almost to the northern outskirts of Sloviansk. Russian forces lost all of this territory in the Kharkiv region in the fall of 2022.
- The 2024 offensive was stopped in the center of Vovchansk itself, after which it lost any connection to plans for capturing Donbas. The “Sever” grouping’s forces, however, maintained contact with the “Zapad” grouping, which had spent years unsuccessfully attacking nearby Kupyansk. The top priority became reaching Velykyi Burluk, in the rear of the Ukrainian grouping defending Kupyansk.
- In the fall of 2025, Ukraine’s command decided to push Russian forces back from Kupyansk, using units that had been defending Vovchansk. Ukrainian forces managed to temporarily liberate central Kupyansk, but at the cost of a sharp escalation around Vovchansk: Russian forces crossed the Vovcha River in the city center and, by year’s end, had begun a slow advance toward Velykyi Burluk.
- In the summer of 2026, Russian forces unexpectedly launched an offensive across the state border east of Vovchansk. At the same time, groups of Russian assault troops began infiltrating south from Vovchansk toward the village of Bilyi Kolodiaz. In September, the Russian Defense Ministry announced that its troops had “closed the encirclement of a major Ukrainian grouping near the border” east of Bilyi Kolodiaz.
- Since then, no evidence has emerged that this encirclement actually exists. Russian assault troops have been spotted in Bilyi Kolodiaz (more precisely, a single assault trooper with a Russian flag). Russian units advancing from east of the border have reached Blahodatne, but a 17-kilometer (11-mile) “gap” remains between Bilyi Kolodiaz and Blahodatne, where no Russian troop presence has been recorded so far.
- Ukrainian forces haven’t experienced any supply shortages so far at the positions supposedly encircled. Judging by published videos, Ukrainian armored vehicles are still operating inside the hypothetical “pocket” even a month after Russia announced that supply lines had been cut.
- Despite all the Russian command’s exaggerations, the situation for Ukrainian forces in this sector continues to deteriorate: they clearly lack the strength to eliminate the Russian assault troops that have broken through into their rear. Ukrainian troops periodically counterattack with small groups of two or three tanks — a pattern that, given how this war is being fought, may point to a serious shortage of infantry and even drones.
- About 15 kilometers (9 miles) separate Velykyi Burluk from the positions where Russian assault troops have been recorded. Because fighting here is taking place without a stable front line, Russian forces could break through to this city, which is critical for supplying Ukrainian forces on the Vovchansk and Kupyansk fronts.

articles.title: NATO Uses Lessons-Learned in Ukraine to Plan Russian Defeat in 3D+ Battlespace
articles.body:
NATO is drafting a strategy designed to defeat a potential Russian attack on its eastern flank quickly and decisively by combining conventional military power with drones and artificial intelligence.
The document, titled “Theory of Victory,” is being developed under NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) Gen. Alexus Grynkewich and is expected to be presented in Poland on Monday, Oct. 12, Bloomberg reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Bloomberg reviewed an unclassified version of the document, which is intended to clarify how NATO would respond if Russian forces entered the territory of an alliance member.
The strategy remains a planning document rather than an indication that NATO believes a Russian conventional attack is imminent.
“The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage,” Grynkewich’s spokesperson, Col. Martin O’Donnell, told Bloomberg.
O’Donnell declined to discuss operational details but said the alliance needed to prepare now to deter aggression and prevail if attacked. He also stressed that NATO remained a “purely defensive” alliance.
Drones and AI would support conventional forces
Under the proposed strategy, NATO would initially seek to stop an incursion using land forces and capabilities developed through its Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative.
These would include low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-assisted targeting integrated with conventional weapons and military units.
Russian Authorities Won’t Confirm Pneumonic Plague Outbreak in Central Siberia
After securing freedom of movement, allied forces would attempt to disrupt and destroy the enemy’s command-and-control structure, with the aim of defeating the attacking forces before they could establish a lasting foothold on NATO territory.
The plan emphasizes avoiding unintended provocations while demonstrating enough military readiness to convince an adversary that an attack could not succeed.
It also covers hybrid threats – hostile actions such as sabotage, cyberattacks, interference with infrastructure and covert operations that remain below the threshold of open warfare.
Russia has reportedly ordered its intelligence services to intensify hybrid operations across NATO and EU countries, including possible sabotage against military facilities, critical infrastructure and communications systems.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said there are currently no indications that Russia is preparing a conventional assault on the alliance. However, European governments expect Moscow’s hybrid campaign to continue and potentially intensify.
NATO applies lessons from Ukraine
The strategy reflects lessons from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, where inexpensive drones, electronic warfare and rapidly updated software have transformed even frontline 2D battlefield operations into 3D-plus battlespace operations.
NATO has already been testing drones, unmanned ground vehicles, counter-drone equipment and new communications systems under the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative.
The alliance has also explored an AI-assisted automated defensive zone along its borders with Russia and Belarus. The proposed system would use interconnected sensors, drones and weapons to detect hostile movements while reducing the number of soldiers required to monitor exposed areas.
In July, NATO members agreed to invest more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities over five years. The alliance is also developing a counter-drone marketplace and plans to train five times as many military drone operators by the end of 2027.
Allies face spending and force decisions
The proposal comes as European NATO members sharply increase defense expenditure but debate how to divide funding between tanks, artillery and other conventional weapons and newer technologies demonstrated in Ukraine.
The US reportedly sent allies a questionnaire during the summer asking about their defense spending and support for President Donald Trump’s policies as Washington considered reducing some American military assets assigned to Europe.
The questionnaire also asked whether NATO members could contribute additional forces to Grynkewich’s defense plans.
“Theory of Victory” is therefore intended not only to describe a possible military response but also to show governments what forces and technologies they would need to finance before a crisis begins.
The initiative comes amid growing concern about Russian drone incursions, sabotage and airspace violations along NATO’s eastern flank. Rutte has said the alliance deliberately keeps the precise threshold for activating Article 5 ambiguous, preventing adversaries from calculating how far they can escalate without triggering a collective response.

articles.title: American bomber fleet departs Britain
articles.body:
All US bombers deployed to RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire have returned to their home stations in the United States, ending the latest sustained deployment of American heavy bombers at the British airbase, according to US European Command.
European Command confirmed on 4 October that the aircraft “are redeploying to their home stations”, while a US Department of Defense official separately confirmed that every American bomber deployed to Fairford had now left the base.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States,” a US Air Force statement said.
The aircraft remaining at Fairford before the departure were B-1B Lancer bombers. The New York Times, citing two US officials, reported that 12 B-1s were involved in the redeployment and that at least three had reached South Dakota by Sunday. No reason for the withdrawal has been given publicly by the Pentagon or US European Command.
European Command said American bombers routinely deploy internationally as part of global readiness and operational requirements, without providing further detail on the decision to bring the Fairford aircraft home. “US Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements,” the US statement said.
The service added that its bomber force remained capable of carrying out long-range operations directly from the continental United States. “The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime.”
RAF Fairford is a Royal Air Force station used extensively by the United States Air Force and serves as a forward operating location for US strategic bomber deployments to Europe. Its long runway and supporting infrastructure allow aircraft including the B-1B Lancer, B-2 Spirit and B-52 Stratofortress to operate from the Gloucestershire base.
The airfield has hosted a substantial US bomber presence during 2026. B-1 and B-52 aircraft operated from Fairford during American military operations connected with the war with Iran, making the base one of the principal European locations supporting the deployment of US long-range strike aircraft.
Six B-52 Stratofortress bombers had already departed Fairford earlier in the year, leaving B-1 Lancers as the remaining deployed bomber force at the base by the beginning of October.
The B-1B is a supersonic long-range conventional bomber operated by the US Air Force. Although originally developed during the Cold War with a nuclear role, the aircraft was subsequently converted to a conventional-only mission and has been used extensively for long-range strike operations.

articles.title: DIU reveals new version of Russian Geran-4 with optics and compass
articles.body:
DIU reveals new version of Russian Geran-4 with optics and compass
According to Ukrinform, the Main Intelligence Directorate reported this.
According to intelligence reports, the upgraded “Geran-4” incorporates a new “MOH” unit, which is based on a high-precision magneto-inductive sensor (magnetometer) PNI5GA manufactured by the American company PNI Sensor. This module works in conjunction with the SADRA inertial navigation module to reduce the drift of its gyroscopes, thereby improving the accuracy of the drone’s autonomous navigation.
In addition to satellite and inertial navigation, the Russians have added another autonomous navigation system—the “Susannin” optoelectronic correlation system, which compares images from an optical sensor with a reference image stored in the computer’s memory, to ensure the drone’s route aligns from the launch point to the target point. A similar system is also used on the new “Geran-5” K5 version.
1 / 5
To effectively destroy (by cutting with a cumulative jet) bridge structures and power line towers, Russian invaders have begun using a new warhead for the KRSN—a special cumulative-cutting payload.
The Russians have replaced the Chinese Telefly turbojet engine with a domestically produced counterpart manufactured in Alabuga.
The rest of the electronic units and components remain unchanged and are identical to those of previous “Geranium” models.
As reported by Ukrinform, thanks to the deployment of their own satellite communications, Russian troops have changed their tactics for jet drone strikes on Kyiv and are now controlling the drones in real time instead of following pre-programmed routes.

Ukraine Develops New Nika Missile to Shoot Down Jet-Powered Shahed Drones
Ukraine has developed a new small missile called Nika to intercept jet-powered Shahed drones, while additional anti-drone turrets are being deployed in Kyiv and the surrounding region, Suspilne reported on October 4.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the new interceptor while speaking with journalists ahead of talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The new systems come as Ukraine works to improve interception rates against faster jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy previously reported that Ukraine was intercepting around 85% to 92% of conventional Shahed drones, while the interception rate for jet-powered UAVs stood at approximately 50% to 60%.

“There will be dozens of these turrets at different facilities, and we will defend ourselves as best we can,” Zelenskyy stated.
The expansion of Ukraine’s air defenses comes as Russian drone and missile strikes continue hitting Ukraine’s critical civilian infrastructure. articles.title: Estonia moves troops closer to Russian border under ‘active defense’ program
articles.body:
Estonia is preparing for possible Russian provocations by moving troops closer to its border with Russia and buying weapons capable of striking deep inside Russian territory, the Financial Times reported.
Under its new “active defense” strategy, Estonia has expanded and modernized a base in Jõhvi, 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the border with Russia. The headquarters of the First Brigade has relocated there from Tapa, Estonia’s main military base, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) from the border.
Estonia is also building a new base in Narva designed to house 1,000 troops. The plan calls for 200 troops to be stationed there permanently, while the base could accommodate another 800 in the event of a crisis on the border.
Estonian military officials believe Russia is unlikely to try to seize the border town of Narva but do not rule out provocations meant to test how NATO’s collective defense clause functions.
As part of the “active defense” strategy, Estonia signed contracts in 2025 to buy nine American-made HIMARS systems with missiles that have a range of up to 300 kilometers (186 miles), as well as nine South Korean Chunmoo multiple rocket launchers with a similar range, the Financial Times reported.
Military and intelligence officials believe Russia is not ready for a full-scale war with NATO, at least not within the next couple of years, the FT reported, but they intend to do everything possible “to make aggression against us unthinkable.” “Our aim is clear: to keep the enemy and the destruction of war away from Estonian territory,” the Defense Ministry said.
European countries, especially those bordering Russia, have said repeatedly in recent months that they fear Russian provocations designed to pressure NATO into abandoning its support for Ukraine. Latvia’s intelligence services made a similar statement in the summer of 2026.

articles.title: Russia Upgrades Geran-4 Drones With Better Navigation and New Warhead, Ukraine Says
articles.body:
Russia has upgraded its Geran-4 attack drones with technology designed to make them harder to disrupt and more accurate, Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) agency said.
The new version, which Russia has started using this autumn, can navigate more precisely without relying entirely on satellite signals and carries a new warhead designed to damage bridges and power infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
One of the upgrades is a small magnetic sensor made by US company PNI Sensor. It helps the drone understand changes in its position and correct errors in its onboard navigation system, improving its ability to stay on course.
Russia has also added an optical navigation system called “Susanin.” In simple terms, the system uses a camera to compare what the drone sees below with images stored in its computer.
This allows the drone to recognize where it is and follow its planned route even without relying on GPS or other satellite navigation.
A similar system is being used on the newer Geran-5 drone, according to Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
The upgraded Geran-4 also carries a new warhead designed specifically to attack infrastructure. It can use a powerful shaped charge to cut through bridge structures and supports carrying high-voltage power lines.
Russia has also replaced the Chinese-made engine previously used on the drone with a Russian-made version produced at the Alabuga industrial facility in Russia’s Tatarstan.
Guterres’s Successor Will Need Russia’s Blessing
Most of the drone’s other electronic components remain unchanged, HUR said in a report published on its War&Sanctions portal.
What is the Geran-4?
The Geran-4 is a relatively large, jet-powered attack drone designed for long-range strikes. It is about 3.6 meters (11.8 feet) long, has a 3.05-meter (10-foot) wingspan and can carry a warhead weighing up to 50 kilograms (110 pounds).
It has a maximum takeoff weight of about 450 kilograms (992 pounds). Its cruising speed is around 320 km/h (200 mph), while its maximum speed is 350 km/h (217 mph).
The drone has a reported range of about 770 kilometers (479 miles) and can fly at altitudes of up to 4 kilometers (2.5 miles).
Geran-4 vs. Geran-5
The Geran-5 is a larger and more powerful member of the same family.
It is about 6.5 meters (21.3 feet) long and weighs up to 850 kilograms (1,874 pounds) – almost twice as much as the Geran-4. It can carry a warhead weighing up to 90 kilograms (198 pounds).
The Geran-5 has a cruising speed of 450–600 km/h (280–373 mph) and a range of about 950 kilometers (590 miles). It can fly at altitudes of up to 6 kilometers (3.7 miles).
In simple terms, the Geran-4 is smaller and lighter, while the Geran-5 is a much larger platform capable of carrying a heavier warhead and flying faster and farther.

Russia’s Tu-95MS Goes Down With Three Officers Linked to Missile Strikes on Ukraine
Three Russian strategic aviation officers linked to missile strikes against Ukraine were among those killed when a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in Russia’s Amur region in late September.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on October 4, the officers were identified as Lieutenant Colonel Fedor Pavlyukov and Majors Andrey Gerasimov and Andrey Lobanov. A photograph of the deceased crew was published by Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky District in the Amur region.
The Tu-95MS crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo on September 29 during what the Russian Defense Ministry described as a training flight. Russian authorities said six crew members were killed and one person survived with injuries.
Pavlyukov served as deputy commander for flight training with Russia’s 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment and previously commanded one of its Tu-95MS squadrons, according to data cited by Militarnyi from the Ukrainian database Book of Executioners. Ukrainian researchers linked him to the preparation and execution of missile strikes against Ukraine.
Gerasimov was a Tu-95MS squadron commander with the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, which is associated with Engels-2 airbase in Russia’s Saratov region. According to the same database, he participated in combat sorties and may have been involved in organizing cruise missile launches during strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Lobanov served as deputy commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in Russian military unit 75715. Militarnyi, citing previous reporting by 24 Kanal, said Lobanov commanded a Tu-95MS during a May 29, 2023 combat sortie in which its crew launched six air-launched missiles at Ukrainian critical infrastructure.
The crash occurred as Russia continued moving Tu-95MS bombers between Engels-2 and Ukrainka airbase in the Amur region following Ukrainian strikes against strategic aviation facilities.
According to Militarnyi, Engels-2 is used to prepare aircraft and load Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles, while the more distant Ukrainka base allows Russia to disperse its strategic aviation fleet. Such deployments can require flights exceeding 12,000 kilometers and lasting close to 24 hours.
The Soviet-designed Tu-95MS remains one of Russia’s primary strategic missile carriers and has been repeatedly used to launch Kh-101 cruise missiles against Ukraine.
Earlier, on October 1, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter crashed in the Voronezh region, killing all three crew members. The helicopter was reportedly shot down by a Russian Su-35 fighter after being misidentified as a Ukrainian drone during a large-scale drone attack.

articles.title: Ukraine using AI-enabled robot guns to counter Russian drones
articles.body:
Ukraine commenced using artificial intelligence-enabled robot guns to bring down Russia's new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, according to its air force on Monday.
For months, Kyiv has been seeking a way to intercept the new Russian drones pounding the Ukrainian capital, even as it faces a dire lack of suitable ammunition to take them out.
Russia has been deploying newer jet-powered drones that move faster and are harder to intercept than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shahed drones.
As part of Ukraine's efforts to respond, "robotic turrets are now being installed on bridges," air force spokesperson Col. Yuri Ignat told national television.
"There have already been shoot downs," of the drones, including the bigger, faster and more powerful Geran-5 version, he told national television.
Speaking to Agence France-Presse (AFP), Ignat explained that the new turrets, which have been seen by AFP journalists in the Ukrainian capital, use "optical vision and artificial intelligence to eliminate the human factor and deliver strikes."
Sergiy Beskrestnov, a technology adviser to the Ukrainian defense ministry, explained on Telegram over the weekend that the new automated turrets were "an innovative Ukrainian solution that shoots down (drones) using machine guns controlled by artificial intelligence."
He said that 12 of the turrets had been installed in Kyiv, adding that "more turrets will be installed in the future."
Ignat acknowledged that the new system had a small operating radius.
"It can operate at about one kilometer plus (0.6 miles). And it works when conditions are favorable, when the attack approach angle is suitable," he told AFP.
"This is not some kind of panacea," he said, stressing that the turrets were part of "an integrated air defense system that provides engagement of these targets at different tiers."
"Of course, we rely on all available assets."
Ukraine has been accelerating the integration of artificial intelligence into its defense capabilities and is already using the technology on the frontlines to guide drones, detect targets for strikes and coordinate large-scale operations.

articles.title: NATO Drafts "Theory of Victory" Plan Using Drones and AI to Repel Russian Attack

NATO Drafts "Theory of Victory" Plan Using Drones and AI to Repel Russian Attack
NATO’s top military commander is preparing a strategy to quickly defeat any Russian attack on the alliance’s eastern flank, using drones and artificial intelligence alongside conventional forces.
Bloomberg reported the plan on October 5 after reviewing an unclassified version of the document and speaking with senior officials and diplomats familiar with the initiative.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The document, titled "Theory of Victory," is being developed under Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich. He is expected to present the strategy in Poland on October 12.
The plan is intended to clarify how NATO would respond to a potential Russian incursion into allied territory. It places particular emphasis on integrating emerging technologies, including drones and AI, with NATO’s existing conventional military capabilities.
Rather than replacing traditional forces, the strategy seeks to integrate technological systems with established military power to accelerate decision-making on the battlefield and strengthen NATO’s ability to stop an attack before Russia can achieve its initial objectives.
The document comes amid heightened tensions between NATO and Russia and growing concern among allied governments about Moscow’s intentions toward the alliance’s eastern members.
The outlet noted that officials have been assessing repeated reports suggesting Russia could consider military action against NATO territory.
The strategy also reflects NATO’s broader effort to absorb lessons from Russia’s war against Ukraine, where drones, automated targeting, electronic warfare, and rapidly changing battlefield technologies have become central to combat operations.
The alliance has increasingly focused on integrating such capabilities into its eastern defenses while retaining conventional forces as the foundation of deterrence.
NATO's shift toward automated warfare has already begun taking shape along the alliance's eastern flank.
Earlier reports indicated that the alliance plans a unified surveillance and defense system stretching from Finland to the Black Sea, built on drones, satellites, sensors, and AI to detect and help repel incoming attacks.
The approach draws on Ukraine, where AI-guided drone swarms can identify targets and strike autonomously even when Russian electronic warfare severs human control.
During the Freedom Shield 2026 exercises near the Belarusian border, Germany's 45th Armored Brigade fitted its Leopard 2 tanks and Fuchs carriers with anti-drone screens modeled on Ukrainian combat experience.

Estonia Moves Troops Toward Russian Border, Prepares 300-Km Deep Strikes Under New Defense Strategy
Estonia is moving key combat units closer to its border with Russia and expanding its long-range strike capabilities under a new “active defense” strategy aimed at confronting a potential attack from forward positions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Financial Times on October 5, the headquarters of Estonia’s 1st Infantry Brigade—the country’s main combat formation—is being permanently relocated from Tapa to Jõhvi, about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the Russian border, where new military facilities are under construction.
“We have to start at the border and win the first battles,” Colonel Tarmo Kundla, commander of the brigade, told the Financial Times.
The move represents a shift from Estonia’s previous strategy, which envisioned slowing an invading force while waiting for NATO reinforcements. Under the new approach, Estonian forces intend to defend territory from forward positions and strike military targets deep behind enemy lines from the beginning of an attack.
Estonia is also building a military base in Narva, directly on the Russian border. The facility is expected to permanently host about 200 troops and accommodate up to 1,000 personnel during a crisis.
At the same time, Tallinn is expanding its long-range firepower. Estonia is set to field nine US-made HIMARS and nine South Korean K239 Chunmoo launchers, with available munitions capable of reaching approximately 300 kilometers. The Financial Times noted that St. Petersburg is about 260 kilometers from Estonia’s eastern military positions.
“To make deterrence credible, we have to make aggression against us unthinkable. Our goal is clear: keep the enemy and the destructive consequences of war away from Estonian territory,” Estonia’s Defense Ministry said, according to the Financial Times.
The shift comes as Estonia increases defense spending to approximately €2.4 billion in 2026, or about 5.4% of GDP, with €1.27 billion allocated to weapons and other defense procurement.
Estonian intelligence does not currently assess a Russian attack on NATO as imminent. Officials cited by the Financial Times said they do not expect Moscow to seek a full-scale war with NATO within at least the next two years, but warned that Russia’s military restructuring could increase the threat in the longer term.
Earlier, Estonian security officials warned of a pro-Russian influence campaign promoting the creation of a so-called “Narva People’s Republic.” The campaign, reported by BILD in March, included calls for sabotage and armed resistance, with Estonian intelligence warning that it could be intended to prepare the ground for a scenario similar to Russia’s actions in eastern Ukraine in 2014.

The case against Bortko, who called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine, has been brought to court — what punishment does the Russian director face
Kyiv • UNN
The SBU has completed its investigation into Volodymyr Bortko, who called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine and its capture. He faces up to 8 years in prison.
The indictment against Vladimir Bortko, the director of "Bandit Petersburg," who called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine, has been sent to court, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General and the Security Service of Ukraine.
Details
The Security Service of Ukraine has completed its pretrial investigation into Russian director, screenwriter, and former State Duma deputy Vladimir Bortko, who promotes Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine.
The SBU investigators have now submitted the indictment to the court. The offender faces up to 8 years in prison with confiscation of property.
The investigation established that the suspect publicly calls for the continuation of the war, denies Ukrainian statehood, and advocates the use of tactical nuclear weapons against our country.
The SBU recalled that Bortko is known for the Russian television series "Bandit Petersburg" and "Streets of Broken Lanterns." He combined his work in cinema with political support for the Kremlin regime.
During the investigation, Security Service officers documented numerous episodes of his provocative statements between 2017 and 2026.
Thus, on the air of the "Komsomolskaya Pravda" radio station, he once again called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine. In addition, he advocated seizing Kyiv and then the entire territory of our country.
On the basis of the evidence collected, Bortko has been charged under two articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine:
▪️ Article 436 (propaganda of war);
▪️ Part 3 of Article 436-2 (the production and dissemination of materials in which Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine is justified, recognized as lawful, or denied, committed repeatedly and using the mass media).
Since the suspect is located in Russia, comprehensive measures are underway to bring him to justice.
The investigation was conducted under the procedural guidance of the Office of the Prosecutor General.

articles.title: Ukraine says Russian drones behind Turkish ship sinking
articles.body:
Ukraine says Russian drones behind Turkish ship sinking
October 5, 2026
Romanian authorities said on Monday that two people were killed and another one was wounded after a fire broke out in a commercial vessel on Romanian waters in the Black Sea.
The Turkish-owned civilian vessel subsequently sank. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the incident was caused by a Russian drone attack.
Romania's Interior Ministry said the Coast Guard was alerted at around 11 a.m. local time (14:00 UTC) and the afflicted vessel was in Romania's exclusive economic zone, some 30 nautical miles (55 kilometers) south of Sfantul Gheorghe in Tulcea County.
"Eleven crew members have been rescued. Two deceased individuals have also been located," the ministry said, adding that a helicopter had airlifted the injured.
Zelenskyy accuses Russia of 'horrific strike'
Authorities did not identify the cause of the fire, but Romanian media reported that the ship was carrying grain and was hit by a drone.
"A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Türkiye. Azerbaijani and Indian citizens were on board," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X.
"As of now, unfortunately, we know that the ship's captain was killed ... The fate of one other person is still being established," he added.
The Ukrainian government says it has repeatedly proposed taking steps to de-escalate the situation in the Black Sea, which is putting maritime trade at risk.
"But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian vessels instead of normal maritime navigation," Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
Rising threat to Black Sea maritime traffic
The Black Sea is a major commercial shipping route, which connects Ukraine's grain exports with the rest of the world. The waterway has faced heightened security concerns since Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine in 2022.
There has been an increase in war-related objects found in the Black Sea, mostly in Romanian, Bulgarian and Turkish waters, with analysts saying the trend is expected to continue.
The incident is the latest to take place on Romanian waters. In August, a Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed a marine drone near an offshore gas project in the Black Sea.
Two months before, a Ukrainian maritime drone exploded in Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta, with Ukraine saying the drone had been knocked off course by Russian electronic interference.

articles.title: India, Switzerland to work for global peace, stability amid US-Iran, Ukraine wars, says Modi

Ahmad Adil

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Monday that India and Switzerland would work together for global peace and stability amid the US-Iran and Ukraine wars.
The remarks came as Modi hosted Swiss President Guy Parmelin, who is on an official visit to the South Asian nation.
Modi and Parmelin held “wide-ranging discussions” in New Delhi hours after the Swiss president arrived in India, Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal wrote on US social media platform X.
Noting that India and Switzerland believe in “democratic values, rule of law, dialogue and diplomacy,” Modi said: “We will work together for global peace and stability.”
Modi said whether it is Ukraine or the Middle East, India “continues to support every effort towards peace.”
“We also agree that reforms in global institutions are necessary to address the increasing global challenges,” he said.
The Indian prime minister also said the two countries would “develop trusted supply chains and reliable solutions for the entire world.”
“Today we recognized the new possibilities of cooperation in military exchange and defense production. We also agreed to promote cooperation in nuclear energy,” he said.
The Indian Ministry of External Affairs said key outcomes from Monday’s talks included new agreements on “transport, mobility and infrastructure, migration and mobility, and young professionals, alongside new joint research in health, clean energy and space.”
India, which established relations with Switzerland in 1948, recorded bilateral trade of approximately $23.35 billion in 2024-25.

articles.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
articles.body:
On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.
Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.
Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.
Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.
After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.
Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.
“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.
“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”
On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.
“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”
Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.
When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”
The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.
In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.
“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”
With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.
She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.
“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

articles.title: All B-1 Bombers Leave RAF Fairford in Hasty Departure from UK Base
articles.body:
All 12 American bombers deployed in Britain rapidly returned to the U.S. on Oct. 4 following security concerns about a potential Iranian threat to their base in the U.K.
The dozen B-1B Lancer bombers, which were stationed at RAF Fairford amid ongoing hostilities with Iran, departed over the course of a day, local aircraft spotters said. The U.S. military later confirmed the unexpected departure of the aircraft.
“All U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States,” the Pentagon and U.S. European Command said in statements to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The U.S. military emphasized that bombers could still strike targets across the globe from the continental United States—something B-1B, B-2 Spirit, and B-52 Stratofortress bombers all did during the height of operations against Iran this spring.
“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities—including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States—anywhere, anytime,” the statement read.
Still, stationing bombers at RAF Fairford sharply reduced the flight time U.S. bombers needed to strike targets in Iran. The open-source group Military Air Tracking Alliance recorded 29 separate bombers that deployed to RAF Fairford, located in southwest England, at different points during the conflict.
The departure of the last 12 bombers comes a week after arrests were made following a suspected plot against the base. Six people have been arrested in connection with the episode. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were “strong indications” that Iran was behind the threat.
Burnham and his predecessor Keir Starmer allowed the U.S. to use the base to attack Iran for what the U.K. government called defensive strikes. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July it considered RAF Fairford a legitimate target because of the U.S. bombers deployed there.
At the height of the deployment, which began in early March during Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. had around two dozen bombers deployed to RAF Fairford at a single time—some 18 B-1B and half a dozen B-52H bombers. Since the U.S. reached a shaky ceasefire with Iran in April, the bombers have mostly conducted training missions, and the B-52s left months ago. One B-1B that arrived just last week to replace another bomber was part of the exodus on Oct. 4.
RAF Fairford does not have permanent assigned U.S. Air Force aircraft, but the base has a wing dedicated to supporting U.S. operations and is considered the main U.S. bomber site in Europe, having regularly hosted U.S. aircraft for years.
The Air Force permanently stations aircraft in the U.K. at RAF Lakenheath, which hosts F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters that have deployed to the Middle East to operate against Iran. Lakenheath also serves as a stopover for fighters heading to and from the Middle East from the U.S. Nearby, RAF Mildenhall hosts KC-135 tankers that belong to the 100th Air Refueling Wing stationed at the base.
The U.S. has also been rotating its fighters based in the Middle East, sending fresh F-16 Fighting Falcon and F-35 units to the region, primarily from the Air National Guard.

articles.title: ISW analyses why Russia is rushing to strike Ukraine's energy infrastructure

ISW analyses why Russia is rushing to strike Ukraine's energy infrastructure
Analysts from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) have said that Russia is beginning its campaign of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure earlier than usual, before Ukraine can develop effective measures to counter Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
Source: ISW report on 4 October
Details: The report said that the Russian Defence Ministry had set out its main rhetorical justification for the upcoming brutal Russian campaign of strikes against Ukraine's critical infrastructure in the autumn and winter of 2026-2027.
The Russian ministry presented the escalation as a response to "alleged Ukrainian strikes against Russian civilian targets in multiple instances since June 2026".
ISW analysts suggested that Ukraine's battlefield successes in 2026 appear to be "forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to reevaluate his original theory of victory in Ukraine and shift focus to compelling Ukraine to surrender through the winter 2026-2027 long-range strike campaign, as opposed to advances on the battlefield". The report added that this "strike campaign aims to make civilian life in Ukraine unbearable such that Ukraine will capitulate to Russia's demands".
Russia has conducted similar campaigns of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure every winter since the winter of 2022-2023 and is likely to begin its strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure earlier than usual this year, before Ukraine can develop effective measures to counter Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, which have already caused significant damage.
Quote from the report: "The Russian MoD's rhetorical framing is attempting to justify the intensification of its strike campaign, which will target Ukraine's already-degraded energy infrastructure and other critical infrastructure, to Russians and the international community."
Background:
- The Ukrainian Defence Ministry stated that Ukrainian long-range operations have put more than 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity out of action.

articles.title: Three Russian Strategic Aviation Officers Responsible for Missile Strikes on Ukraine Killed in Tu-95MS Crash
articles.body:
Three officers involved in missile strikes on Ukraine were among those killed in the crash of a Russian Tu-95MS strategic bomber in the Amur Region.
A photo of the crew members killed in the crash was published by Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky Municipal District in the Amur Region.
They were Lt. Col. Fedor Pavlyukov and Majors Andrei Gerasimov and Andrei Lobanov.
The crash occurred on September 29, 2026, during a training flight in the Amur Region, near the village of Krasnoyarovo.
According to an official statement by the Russian Defense Ministry, six crew members were killed and another was injured and evacuated to a medical facility.
According to OSINT researcher Duke BG, photographs of eight people killed in the crash are arranged according to their positions within the crew, while the last two were passengers.
One of those killed was Lt. Col. Fedor Pavlyukov. According to the Ukrainian Book of Executioners project, Pavlyukov served as deputy commander for flight training of the 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment. Previously, from August 2021 to April 2024, he commanded a Tu-95MS aviation squadron of the same regiment.
Pavlyukov was responsible for preparing flight crews to carry out combat missions and commanded a unit. Ukrainian researchers link him to the organization and execution of missile strikes against Ukraine.
The 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment is part of the 326th Heavy Bomber Aviation Division and operates Tu-95MS strategic bombers. The 182nd Regiment had about 16 Tu-95MS aircraft.
The second identified officer was Maj. Andrei Gerasimov. According to the Book of Executioners, he was commander of a Tu-95MS aviation squadron of the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division. Before that, from June 2022 to October 2024, he served as deputy squadron commander.
Gerasimov personally took part in combat sorties and may have been involved in organizing and carrying out cruise missile launches during mass strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The 121st Regiment is associated with Engels-2 air base in the Saratov Region, one of Russia’s key strategic aviation airfields. On August 28, long-range drones operated by the SSU’s Special Operations Center “A” hit a Russian Tu-95MS there.
Another person killed was Maj. Andrei Lobanov, deputy commander of a Tu-95MS aviation squadron of military unit 75715. According to 24 Kanal, on May 29, 2023, Lobanov carried out a combat sortie as the commander of a Tu-95MS, during which the crew launched six air-launched missiles in succession at critical infrastructure facilities in Ukraine.
The crash occurred amid a significant workload on Russia’s strategic bomber fleet. Following Ukrainian strikes on strategic aviation airfields, Russia began actively moving Tu-95MS aircraft between Engels-2 air base and Ukrainka in the Amur Region.
At Engels-2, the aircraft can undergo preparation and be armed with Kh-101 cruise missiles before combat sorties, while the remote Ukrainka air base is used, among other purposes, to disperse strategic aviation and reduce its vulnerability to Ukrainian attacks.
As a result, the bombers have to make lengthy flights between the Russian Far East and the European part of Russia. The total range of an individual combat sortie can exceed 12,000 kilometers, while its duration can approach 24 hours.
Such a workload accelerates wear on the aircraft, many of which were manufactured during the Soviet era, while also increasing the burden on flight crews and maintenance personnel.
