articles.title: US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot
articles.body:
The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the US, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity.
A Pentagon spokesperson said: “While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.”
At least 10 B-1 bombers of 12 flew out of Fairford on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure and the apparent significance given by the US to the threat.
There was no immediate comment from the UK Ministry of Defence, though the rapid pace of the withdrawal will heighten concerns in the area around the RAF base in Gloucestershire.
According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base.
A report in the New York Times said: “American officials on Sunday declined to specify the nature of the new information that prompted the rapid withdrawal of the Air Force bombers, some of which had just arrived in the past week as part of a normal rotation of forces.
“One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but specific details and a sense of urgency spiked in the past 24 hours, alarming commanders.”
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement.
RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160km) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
Its use in recent months came after then prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran.
The US military still maintains a sizeable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a US official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier as well as the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group – a group of ships that together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines – were heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers being in the region as early as the end of October.

articles.title: Estonia moves troops closer to Russia in preparation for active defense: Report
articles.body:
Seyma Erkul Dayanc
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Estonia is moving military units closer to its border with Russia and expanding its long-range strike capabilities as part of a new “active defense” strategy, The Financial Times reported Monday, according to broadcaster ERR.
The First Brigade of the Estonian Defense Forces is being permanently relocated from Tapa to Johvi, about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the Russian border.
New facilities are being built in Johvi to accommodate the brigade.
Estonia is also building a military base in Narva, a city near the Russian border, with capacity for up to 1,000 personnel in a crisis.
Estonian military and intelligence officials told the financial daily that they do not expect Russia to launch a full-scale war with NATO within the next two years but are preparing for possible future conflict and concerned about a potential limited-scale operation against Estonia.
Estonia has signed contracts for nine US-made HIMARS multiple rocket launchers, including missiles with ranges of up to 300 km (186 mi), and is also acquiring nine South Korean Chunmoo systems with similar ranges, the report said.
Estonia’s defense spending is expected to rise 42% this year to €2.4 billion ($2.8 billion), or 5.4% of gross domestic product.

articles.title: Yemen air campaign against Houthis under way, says Saudi-led coalition
articles.body:
Leaders of a Saudi-led coalition in Yemen claimed a broad air campaign involving 100 jet aircraft was under way on Monday against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coastline and farther north in the capital, Sana’a.
The Saudi coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the 100 fighter jets participating in Operation Dawn of Yemen were providing support to forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets. He claimed hundreds of Houthi fighters had been besieged in the Dhubab district, including the airport, close to the Bab al-Mandab strait, with some Houthi fighters fleeing across the Red Sea in boats.
Southern Yemeni forces known as the Giants Brigades, who are allied with the government, earlier on Monday launched a ground offensive against the rebels on the eastern flank of the coastal areas that the Houthis seized in their latest advances. The government forces also claim to have cut the road between Mocha and Dhubab, and that Houthi forces were deserting the recently captured city of Mocha as residents stayed behind closed doors.
Previous Saudi-led statements about territorial gains in recent weeks have often proved partial, but footage appeared to back up the Saudi claims of Houthis retreating by the seashore.
The president of the Saudi-backed government, Rashad al-Alimi, had promised a new offensive on Sunday, saying patience with the Houthis had run out. “Today we are embarking on a decisive phase in the history of our nation,” he said.
Airstrikes were also reported on Monday in Sana’a and the Houthi stronghold of Saada in the north of Yemen. Command and control centres, camps and weapons depots were targeted.
The Houthis, who captured Sana’a in 2014, have in recent weeks made lightning advances down the west coast of Yemen, reaching the Bab al-Mandab and seizing strategic islands on the strait.
On Monday Houthi sources denied reports of a retreat, and pointed to the explosions at a Saudi Aramco plant in Riyadh as a sign of the damage the group could still inflict on exposed Saudi oil installations, and by extension the world economy.
It appears a political agreement reached between the two main external Arab actors in Yemen – Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – permitted the UAE-backed Southern Giants to coordinate with the Saudi air force in the attack towards the coast.
It is being stressed by the Giants Brigades that no other ground forces supporting the Saudi-backed government are involved in the offensive. The brigades, who are linked with the Southern Transitional Council, a political group outlawed in Yemen for trying to set up a secessionist state, are certain to have sought political commitments about the future status of Yemen in order to have thrown their military weight behind it.
It is not clear how the Saudis propose to address the age-old southern question. Concessions to the Southern Transitional Council (STC) about the future governance of the south are certain to have been demanded, even if the UAE itself does not return to Yemen.
But the cooperation between the Saudi air force and the Giants Brigades is a remarkable turnaround, since as recently as January the Saudi air force was bombing UAE shipments of arms arriving in southern Yemen for STC-backed forces.
The Saudi bombing triggered the UAE pullout from Yemen in January, the sudden dissolution of the STC, and the exile of its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi. At the weekend his supporters vowed to hold demonstrations later this month in support of the return to a separate southern state.
Houthi government officials claimed British fighter jets were supporting the Saudi air force with refuelling, something the UK Ministry of Defence has already announced.
The fighting was under way as senior ministers from Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh to discuss the support Saudi Arabia might need to protect itself from the Houthis. They have formed a joint defence pact but it is not known how it will operate.

articles.title: Ukraine says its strikes have knocked out more than 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity
articles.body:
Ukraine's Security and Defense Forces have "put out of action" more than 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity through recent long-range strikes, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said in a statement published by the Defense Ministry on 4 October. These "carefully thought-out" actions were aimed at "bleeding the Russian war machine" and "destroying its military-economic potential," Khmara said.
Ukraine treats Russia's refineries as a priority target because their revenue helps fund the war. Even Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed on 1 October that the strikes had cost Russia 1% of its GDP and had "partially" achieved their goal, Interfax reported.
The ministry did not publish how it calculated the figure.
"The consequences of Ukrainian operations are not always visible immediately. But the effect accumulates and produces a tangible result," the ministry said.
Ukrainian deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory
The ministry named eight recently struck facilities, among others. One of them is the Moscow Oil Refinery, which Ukraine targeted in a massive drone attack on the night of 20 September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The refinery, operated by Gazprom Neft in Moscow's Kapotnya district, supplies about 40% of Moscow's fuel market and 70% of the Moscow region's demand for gasoline and aviation fuel, according to Russian news Telegram channel Astra.
Another was KINEF, which Ukraine has attacked repeatedly. It is Russia's second-largest oil refinery by capacity, and the Ukrainian military struck it on the night of 30 August, setting off a fire at the facility.
The ministry also named the Yaroslavl, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, and Syzran refineries and the Ust-Luga port complex.
Ukraine triples production and procurement of long-range drones—and this is not the end
This year, Ukraine has tripled the production and procurement of long-range attack drones, the ministry said.
"This is not the limit. We will continue to scale up deep-strike capabilities," the statement said.
International cooperation is part of that push. Berlin will fund the production of additional DeepStrike-class long-range drones in Ukraine, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said after a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group on 15 April. The sides also agreed to jointly develop and produce a medium- and long-range drone system.
Ukraine and Germany also signed an agreement on the joint production of Bars drones, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on 8 July. The Bars' modular design allows it to be used for deep strikes, among other missions.
Oil refinery output has fallen
Russian refineries cut crude oil processing by 14% in the first nine months of the year compared with the same period last year amid Ukrainian drone attacks, according to calculations by two industry sources.
Experts' estimates of the decline differ widely. In August, Serhii Vakulenko of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center put it at 25–28%, while Russian economic commentator Vyacheslav Shiryaev put it at 65–70%, according to Defense-Aerospace.
Fuel production data give a more concrete picture: in July, Russia's gasoline and diesel output was about a quarter to a third lower than in March 2026, the outlet reported.

articles.title: Geran-4 Gets Russian Engine and New Navigation System — DIU
articles.body:
Russia’s Geran-4 jet-powered drone has received a locally produced engine and a new optical navigation system.
The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine reported this on the War&Sanctions portal.
Russian forces began using an upgraded version of this UAV in the fall of this year.
A new MOKH module based on the high-precision PNI5GA magneto-inductive sensor manufactured by U.S. company PNI Sensor has been integrated into the Geran-4 design.
The sensor operates together with the SADRA inertial module, reducing gyroscope drift and improving the accuracy of autonomous navigation.
In addition to satellite and inertial navigation, the enemy has added the Susanin electro-optical correlation system.
It compares images from an optical sensor with a reference image stored in the computer’s memory to adjust the route from the launch point to the target.
Instead of the Chinese Telefly TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine, Russians installed a locally produced equivalent manufactured in Alabuga.
According to Oboronka, engines assembled in Russia undergo additional testing and modifications due to poor manufacturing quality in China. Among the debris, investigators found a turbocharger impeller with Russian markings and drilled holes for weight balancing. Such modifications reduce the centrifugal force acting on the component at high rotational speeds and lower vibrations that can lead to engine failure.
To effectively strike bridge structures and power transmission line towers, the enemy has equipped the drone with a new KRSN shaped-charge cutting warhead.
The remaining electronic modules and components of the UAV remain identical to those used in previous versions of the Geran drones.
The Geran-4 jet-powered attack UAV features a flying-wing aerodynamic configuration and is designed to strike targets at medium and long ranges. The fuselage is approximately 3 meters long, the wingspan exceeds 2.5 meters, and the launch weight is estimated at 200–250 kg, with a warhead weighing up to 50 kg.
The drone is equipped with a turbojet engine that enables it to reach a flight speed of 400–500 km/h and provides an effective range of 400–600 km. Its onboard control system combines satellite navigation, an inertial module, a magnetometric unit, and an electro-optical correction system for autonomous guidance to the target.

articles.title: Russia names eight fatalities in Tu-95MS crash in the Far East, The Insider confirms three officers linked to combat missions in Ukraine
articles.body:
Eight Russian service members — rather than the six initially reported by the Ministry of Defense — were killed on Sept. 29 when a Tu-95MS long-range bomber crashed in the Amur Region. The Insider has established that at least three long-range aviation officers were among the dead: Andrei Lobanov, Fedor Pavlyukov, and Andrei Gerasimov. Ukraine links all three to Tu-95MS combat missions.
On Oct. 4, the local outlet Port Amur was the first to report that the death toll had risen to eight, adding that nine service members had been on board and that two of the dead had not been found right away. Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky District in the Amur Region, soon published a photograph featuring portraits of those killed. The Ministry of Defense had initially reported six dead and one hospitalized.
According to the captions under the portraits, the dead include Andrei Lobanov, Vladislav Moskovskikh, Artur Enokyan, Mikhail Kotyshev, Sergei Moisevich, Vladimir Kelip, Fedor Pavlyukov, and Andrei Gerasimov. Piven said local authorities intend to ask the long-range aviation command to put the crew forward for state honors.
Three of the dead appeared in a Ukrainian database
The Insider cross-checked the data on those killed against the Ukrainian database Russian Torturers, a project launched in 2022 on the initiative of President Volodymyr Zelensky. Its creators say the entries are verified by Ukrainian law enforcement or intelligence agencies.
As of November 2025, Major Andrei Lobanov was listed in the database as deputy commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in Russia’s 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, based at Ukrainka airfield. The database claims that he directly commanded the unit and personally took part in combat missions.
Lieutenant Colonel Fedor Pavlyukov is listed as deputy commander for flight training for the same 182nd Regiment. From August 2021 to April 2024, he commanded a Tu-95MS squadron. The database’s creators say Pavlyukov was responsible for preparing flight crews for combat missions and directly commanded the unit. As early as March 2022, Ukrainian intelligence had placed Pavlyukov on a list of Russian long-range aviation pilots suspected of direct participation in the war against Ukraine.
Major Andrei Gerasimov is listed as commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment. The database claims he directly commanded the unit and personally took part in combat missions.
Ukrainian serviceman and blogger Anatoliy Shtefan (“Stirlitz”) also claimed that at least three of those killed were involved in organizing and carrying out missile strikes on Ukraine, though he did not specify which of those killed he had in mind.
The Sept. 29 plane crash
The Tu-95MS crashed on Sept. 29 during a training flight near the village of Krasnoyarovo in the Mazanovsky District. The Ministry of Defense said the plane had been flying without weapons and went down “in an uninhabited area.” The local government in the Amur Region said the crew steered the aircraft away from residential areas in order to avoid causing further casualties, and no one on the ground was hurt. The ministry sent an Aerospace Forces commission to investigate the crash. No publicly confirmed findings have established its cause.
Ukrainka airfield, where the 182nd Regiment is based, has taken on particular importance for Russia’s long-range aviation over the past year. The Insider previously reported that most of Russia’s long-range bombers (that are still able to fly) were redeployed from the western part of the country to the Far East following Ukraine’s behind-the-lines Operation Spiderweb.
As a result, Ukrainka became the main base for operational Tu-95MS aircraft, significantly complicating combat missions. In order to launch missiles at targets in Ukraine, the aircraft must fly upwards of 12,000 kilometers round-trip, refueling at the Engels or Olenya air bases in western Russia. A typical mission thus lasts around 23 hours, putting significant strain on the aging aircraft.

articles.title: Swiss scammed out of millions by Ukraine-linked call centers – media
articles.body:
Ukraine’s scam-call networks targeting Swiss – anti-fraud squad
Swiss police are investigating a sprawling fraud operation with suspected links to Ukrainian scam call centers, an industry said to be worth billions to corrupt officials in Kiev, Neue Zurcher Zeitung (NZZ) has reported, citing law enforcement officials.
According to a report on Sunday, NEDIK, the police network coordinating Switzerland’s fight against digital crime, recently recorded an increase in fraud offenses suspected of having links to Ukraine. The network declined to provide nationwide figures “for tactical reasons,” but noted that at least four fraudulent call centers in Ukraine have been identified in international investigations involving Swiss authorities, with Swiss and German citizens among their main victims.
One investigation by Bern authorities, reportedly underway for years, concerns a man suspected of operating several call centers in Kiev. On just one platform allegedly linked to the operation, reported losses in Switzerland amounted to nearly 4 million Swiss francs ($4.8 million).
Several Ukrainian nationals have also recently been arrested in Swiss cantons for allegedly acting as cash collectors in telephone scams. In St. Gallen in early September, a person posing as a bank employee called a 93-year-old man and instructed him to withdraw and hand over a large sum of money. Police later arrested a 38-year-old Ukrainian who allegedly collected the cash.
Police in Aargau have similarly reported a growing number of suspected cash collectors holding Ukrainian citizenship. Authorities, however, have not established whether they are being directed by call centers in Ukraine or acting independently. NZZ noted that it remains unclear to what extent Ukraine-based operations are connected to fraud networks and cash collectors operating in Switzerland.
While Russians have long been portrayed as the main targets of Ukrainian scammers, sources cited by NZZ challenged that narrative. Brian Lee, head of the Eurasia Observatory at the Geneva-based Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), said Russians accounted for just 10%-15% of targets even at the height of the so-called “patriotic fraud” narrative, under which young Ukrainians were recruited into scam networks on the pretext of taking revenge for Moscow’s military operation against the Kiev regime. Victims have been identified in at least 29 countries, with scam centers increasingly targeting Europe and the US, according to a GI-TOC report published earlier this year.
Lee also reported that bribing Ukrainian officials for protection is central to the business model, saying GI-TOC investigations found that criminal elements “operate seamlessly and efficiently alongside law enforcement agencies, public officials and the private sector.” Such protection reportedly costs scam operators $10,000-$15,000 per month.
Scam networks and state structures
Corruption has long plagued Ukraine, with high-level scandals including last year’s $100 million Energoatom kickback scheme, reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky. Western-backed investigators have since uncovered further graft involving Ukrainian officials.
The scam call center network reentered the spotlight last month after Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko – a key pillar of Zelensky’s increasingly fragile governing structure – resigned amid the exposure of an industrial-scale network across the country with alleged links to senior figures in Kiev. Ukraine’s Western-backed National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) accused Sergey Kropiva, head of the cybercrime unit at the Prosecutor General’s Office, of leading a ring that collected protection payments from notorious Ukrainian scam call centers. NABU said it identified assets worth almost $1 million allegedly purchased with proceeds from the scheme.
The sums involved in Ukraine’s wider scam industry are reportedly far larger. Ukrainian media earlier estimated that roughly 2,000 scam offices were operating nationwide as of early August, about half paying protection money to corrupt officials. Such payments were estimated at $240 million annually, while the industry itself has been valued at up to $1 billion a month.
The scam industry has also been linked to powerful security structures under Zelensky’s government. In September, personnel from the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and military intelligence (HUR) exchanged fire in Kiev in a confrontation that left three servicemen injured. The clash centered on Stepan Kaplunov, a member of an HUR-linked armed unit detained by the SBU. A law enforcement source cited by Ukrainian outlet Strana said Kaplunov may have been involved in operating scam call centers, pointing to a broader struggle between rival security agencies over the lucrative industry. Ukrainian journalists have also reported that proceeds from criminal operations help finance parts of the HUR’s activities.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has described phone scams as a key tactic employed by Kiev to extract money from Russian citizens, suggesting the practice has effectively become state policy. Moscow considers the industry a national security threat and claims Ukrainian scam networks operate in coordination with the country’s intelligence services.
Russian forces have recently intensified strikes on Ukrainian telecommunications infrastructure, mobile operators, and data centers in response to Kiev’s botched “pressure campaign” of drone attacks on civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia. The strikes have disrupted internet access, digital television, and other services, including by hitting data centers in Kiev that Moscow says were used by Ukrainian military and intelligence services. Media reports late last month also claimed a Russian strike hit one of the scam call centers in Dnepropetrovsk.

articles.title: Discussion on whether to shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine is ongoing, Polish foreign minister says
articles.body:
Discussion on whether to shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine is ongoing, Polish foreign minister says
A discussion is still underway over whether Poland should agree to Ukraine's request to shoot down Russian drones over Ukrainian territory.
Source: Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski speaking to journalists, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sikorski said Poland is changing its rules on the use of force in the border area with Ukraine. However, Poland cannot unilaterally decide to shoot down aerial assets directly over Ukrainian territory.
Quote: "Personally, I understand Ukraine's request to shoot down drones over its territory. I believe that drones or missiles that pose a direct threat to our border constitute a hostile act and therefore provide grounds for self-defence. However, as you know, NATO has established an integrated defence system for the entire eastern flank. This means that the decision does not depend on Poland alone. So the discussion is ongoing, but we have not yet reached the decisions that would satisfy you."
Background:
- Poland recently announced that from 1 October it is changing its air defence procedures in response to Russian airstrikes on Ukraine. The changes concern simplified rules for detecting and shooting down foreign aerial assets in Polish airspace.
- Poland is also preparing a law on a "pre-war state", which is intended to establish rules for action in a situation where the country is not formally at war but the level of threat is already significantly higher than in peacetime.

articles.title: Bloomberg: NATO developing "Theory of Victory" over Russia using drones and AI
articles.body:
Bloomberg: NATO developing "Theory of Victory" over Russia using drones and AI
NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich is developing a strategy for achieving a swift victory in the event of a Russian attack on the Alliance's eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defence technologies such as drones and artificial intelligence.
Source: Bloomberg, which obtained an unclassified version of the document titled Theory of Victory, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Grynkewich is due to present the document in Poland on 12 October. Officials and diplomats familiar with the matter said it is intended to explain how the Alliance would respond to a potential invasion of NATO territory.
The document is also intended to show allies how NATO will integrate conventional weapons with new capabilities that have emerged since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, as well as to encourage greater defence investment and better preparedness, the sources said.
The strategy emphasises NATO's defensive nature and the need to avoid unintended provocations, while making clear the need for a collective response to hybrid threats.
The strategy stresses that by demonstrating its readiness, NATO aims to convince an adversary that victory is impossible.
However, if NATO is attacked, the Alliance would seek to halt the invasion using a combination of ground forces and other assets under the NATO Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative – a concept based on the use of low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-powered targeting.
Grynkewich's spokesperson, Colonel Martin O'Donnell, declined to discuss the details of the plan but stressed that the Alliance is "purely defensive".
"The Supreme Allied Commander Europe's theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO's advantage. Given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked," he said.
Background:
- Martin Jäger, head of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service, has said he sees a risk of violent conflict with Russia and that the confrontation has taken on a new and dangerous quality.
- Media reports have also indicated that Estonia is relocating a key brigade from the town of Tapa to Jõhvi, 50 kilometres from the Russian border, as part of the launch of an "active defence" strategy in preparation for possible Russian aggression.
- Meanwhile, Lithuania and Poland are jointly developing an international civilian evacuation plan that could be implemented if some residents of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia need to be evacuated across the border.

articles.title: Ukraine believes Russia shared jet-drone technology with North Korea, says Zelensky
articles.body:
Ukraine believes Russia shared jet-drone technology with North Korea, says Zelensky
The Ukrainian president on Sunday said Russia shared the technology ‘because North Korea helped them with missiles’
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday he believed Russia may have shared jet-drone technology with its long-standing ally North Korea.
In recent weeks, Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-drones against Ukraine, which so far has no effective means of countering them other than using combat aircraft.
Earlier in the war, North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities.
Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea the technology behind its latest generation of jet-powered drones, Zelensky told journalists: “Yes, of course.”

Kyiv • UNN
On the night of October 5, Russia launched 205 drones at Ukraine. Air defense shot down or suppressed 172 UAVs; hits were recorded in 13 locations.
Russia struck Ukraine with 205 drones during the night of October 5, of which 172 were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Where and with what the enemy attacked
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 5 (from 18:00 on October 4), the enemy attacked with 205 Shahed-type attack UAVs (49 of them jet-powered), Gerbera, "Bandероль"/"Dan-T", and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Orel, Kursk, Shatalovo, Millerovo, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russian Federation, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske.
How many were destroyed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 172 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types. Hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 13 locations, as well as the falling of downed targets (debris) at 3 locations

articles.title: Russia burned 628,000 new school textbooks in Kharkiv at the peak of back-to-school season
articles.body:
Russian missiles and drones destroyed 13 million Ukrainian books this summer, The Guardian reported. That is about a third of all books printed in Ukraine this year, the government estimates.
Russia is striking civilian warehouses, including those where publishers store their books. The uncertainty is pushing publishers toward safe international bestsellers, Publishers Weekly reported. "We'll all end up fed up with safe, non-risky books—if there are still publishers around to publish them," said Iryna Baturevych, co-founder of the publishing news outlet Chytomo.
Millions of Ukrainian books on fire
Ranok is one of Ukraine's largest publishing houses and a leader in children's literature and school textbooks. On one day in August, Russia destroyed more than 85% of its stock, The Guardian reported.
Viktor Kruhlov, the publisher's co-founder and chief executive, was on the warehouse floor at its headquarters in Kharkiv. The facility, built on the site of a former bread factory, covered about 10,000 m².
Together with five senior colleagues, he was discussing plans for the upcoming school year, the peak of the distribution season. Moments after the meeting began, a strike hit about 30 meters from where the staff had gathered. Kruhlov heard an explosion and almost at once saw a huge fire. As colleagues tried to put out the flames, a second strike came, and he realized there could be a third and a fourth, so the staff evacuated. Fifty people were on shift that day, and no one was injured, Kruhlov told The Guardian.
Eight million books, including 628,000 new school textbooks, were in the warehouse at the time. None could be saved. Firefighters battled the blaze for a week.
Several editorial staff members who saw the remains of the warehouse for the first time looked shaken as they recognized fragments of books they had helped create.
"When you see what was produced with your brain, with your hands, with your imagination, spoiled by Russia, it's an awful feeling," Kruhlov said.
He predicted shortages at Ranok's stores this fall, when the books in stock run out and there is nothing to replace them.
Literature is part of Ukrainian identity
Kruhlov is convinced that Russia deliberately targeted the book warehouse, but Bohdana Laiuk, Ukraine's deputy culture minister, sees the strikes as part of Russia's broader campaign against warehouses, The Guardian wrote.
"They cannot occupy Kyiv. So they target warehouses around Kyiv to take the possibility of everyday life from us—and books are part of everyday life," she said.
Books also matter to Russia's occupiers, Laiuk said.
"When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do—and we know this from the areas that were occupied and then liberated in 2022 in the Kherson and Kharkiv regions—is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books out, and destroy them," Laiuk said.
Before 2022, about 70% of the Ukrainian book market consisted of Russian-language titles, most of them imported from Russia.
Russian dominance in Ukrainian publishing developed over centuries, from tsarist bans on publishing in Ukrainian in the 19th century to Soviet Russification. Ukrainian writers were purged, and Ukrainian literature stayed in the shadow of Russian literature, the article notes.
Laiuk calls the dominance of Russian books a form of colonialism. Russia deliberately built its own information space in Ukraine through books, media, and television, she argues, so that everything would be ready for it once its tanks arrived.
Even after independence, a commercially successful Ukrainian-language novel was long seen as unlikely. But at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukrainian bookstores stopped selling Russian imports, and interest in Ukrainian literature grew, from 1920s classics and poetry to contemporary authors and translations.
"So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are," Laiuk told The Guardian in 2023.
The future of Ukrainian literature is uncertain
Ranok is now rushing to reprint textbooks and bestsellers: schools need the former, while sales of popular titles will help the publisher make up for lost revenue.
For debut authors and writers of less commercial or experimental books, the situation is particularly difficult. Even before the strike on Ranok's warehouse, some publications had been delayed by attacks on printing infrastructure.
Ksenia Shpak's debut novel, an urban fantasy about a girl displaced from eastern Ukraine to the Carpathians, was due out in February 2025 but was published only that November, the article says. Half of the print run was in Ranok's Kharkiv warehouse when it was attacked.
It was her first published book, and Shpak fears the publisher will now focus on bestsellers and reprint her novel only if money allows. The Ukrainian book market is also feeling demand level off and the cost of living rise, she said.
Despite the loss of 8 million books, Kruhlov remained optimistic. Looking over the ruined warehouse in Kharkiv, he said he planned to rebuild everything—and to do it better.

articles.title: Germany facing potential ‘violent conflict’ with Russia – spy chief
articles.body:
Germany facing potential ‘violent conflict’ with Russia – spy chief
Germany could become “embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia,” the country’s foreign intelligence chief has warned, claiming that a mysterious drone incident at Leipzig airport is an example of the “real and imminent” threat posed by Moscow.
Speaking to lawmakers at a parliamentary hearing on Monday, Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) head Martin Jaeger declared that “the confrontation we are facing with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous dimension.”
“Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia – the attempted attack in Leipzig is just one example,” he continued, referring to the discovery of an explosive-laden drone next to a Ukrainian transport plane at the city’s airport in August.
German authorities have not released any evidence linking the incident to Russia, and Moscow has described the episode as a “hastily cobbled-together provocation” serving “exclusively the aims of Kiev and the militaristic wing of the European political class.” It is “obvious that Germany is pursuing a further course of escalation,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last month.
Nevertheless, Jaeger claimed that Russia is “waging a shadow war,” and that there is a “real and imminent” threat of attacks against targets in Germany. “No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany,” he added.
Jaeger is one of dozens of Western political, military, and media figures to accuse Russia of waging a “hybrid war” or “shadow war” against Europe in recent weeks. The accusations are, by their nature, impossible to verify, and Moscow has written them off as pretexts to deepen Western involvement in the Russia-Ukraine conflict, justify military spending hikes, and expand surveillance and persecution of domestic opponents.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has explicitly and without evidence described the country’s most popular political party, the right-wing AfD, as “Russia-backed.” Martina Rosenberg, the head of Germany’s Military Counterintelligence Service (MAD), alluded to this claim during Monday’s briefing, telling lawmakers that the country is “threatened by diverse dangers from both outside and within.”
Jaeger, Rosenberg, and domestic intelligence (BfV) chief Sinan Selen all praised Merz’s recent efforts to grant the BND greater offensive powers, and called for further strengthening of the MAD and BfV’s capabilities.
Despite their allegations of “hybrid war,” European leaders have repeatedly stressed that they do not believe Russia to be planning any actual attacks on NATO territory. The BND has seen “no indication of an imminent large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory,” Jaeger added on Monday.
Amid an unprecedented escalation in the West’s rhetoric toward Russia, RT is tracking the statements, accusations, and threats in our ongoing ‘Escalation Watch’ special. Keep an eye on it here as we sort the facts from the propaganda and debunk the psyops in real time.

articles.title: American rocket artillery opens fire in joint drill
articles.body:
US Army rocket artillery has opened fire during a joint live-fire exercise with the Singapore Armed Forces, with M270 Multiple Launch Rocket Systems used during Exercise Daring Warrior 2026 at Fort Sill in Oklahoma, according to the US Army.
Soldiers from Bravo Battery, 3rd Battalion, 13th Field Artillery Regiment, 75th Field Artillery Brigade conducted the firing on 21 September alongside Singaporean personnel as part of the bilateral training event.
Imagery released by the US military shows an M270 launching rockets across the Fort Sill training area, with American and Singaporean troops also working together around artillery equipment and command systems during the exercise.
The US Army said the live-fire was designed to synchronise American and Singaporean launch crews, allowing the two forces to practise delivering coordinated precision fires while testing their ability to operate together on the range. Exercise Daring Warrior brings together artillery personnel from the two countries for training involving weapons operation, command and control and the coordination required to employ long-range fires as part of a combined force.
The M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System is a tracked rocket artillery platform operated by the US Army and several allied militaries. Its launcher carries interchangeable rocket and missile pods, allowing it to employ different types of ammunition depending on the mission.
Unlike conventional tube artillery, multiple launch rocket systems are intended to deliver fires over greater distances and can engage targets using guided munitions. The M270 shares ammunition with the wheeled M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, better known as HIMARS, although the tracked M270 carries two launch pods rather than one.
The system has also gained renewed prominence during the war in Ukraine, where M270 and HIMARS launchers supplied by Western countries have been used extensively by Ukrainian forces for long-range precision strikes.
For the American and Singaporean troops at Fort Sill, the emphasis was on operating the systems as part of a combined artillery force rather than simply conducting individual launcher firings.
Photographs from the exercise show personnel from both armies working together during equipment familiarisation and planning activity, as well as operating observation and targeting equipment in the field. Other imagery shows American and Singaporean troops positioned around command posts and tactical vehicles before the live-fire phase, reflecting the wider chain of activity required to identify targets, pass firing information and coordinate launch crews.
The Singapore Armed Forces operates its own M142 HIMARS rocket artillery systems, giving its personnel experience with a weapons family that shares ammunition and elements of fire-control architecture with the M270.
Fort Sill is the US Army’s principal artillery training centre and home to the Field Artillery School, making the Oklahoma installation a regular location for both domestic and multinational artillery exercises. The 75th Field Artillery Brigade is also based at Fort Sill and provides long-range precision fires capabilities to US forces, with subordinate units operating rocket and missile artillery systems.

articles.title: Estonia to Move Troops to Russian Border Under “Active Defense” Strategy
articles.body:
Estonia is moving some of its troops closer to the Russian border as part of a new “active defense” strategy.
The Financial Times reports that the main units of Estonia’s 1st Infantry Brigade, the country’s main combat force, will be permanently stationed in Jõhvi instead of Tapa.
Jõhvi is located about 50 km from the Russian border, while Tapa is approximately 130 km away.
To accommodate the troops in Jõhvi, Estonia is building new military facilities. The country is also constructing a military base in Narva that will be able to accommodate up to 1,000 troops.
Around 200 troops are expected to be stationed there in peacetime, with up to 800 more deployed in the event of war.
The changes are part of a broader review by Estonia’s Ministry of Defense of its military strategy, as the country shifts to an “active defense” concept introduced in May 2026.
The concept calls for defending the country directly from the border and attempting to stop an enemy at the earliest stage of an attack. As part of this approach, Estonia is acquiring modern weapons and long-range artillery, including HIMARS multiple launch rocket systems.
Militarnyi previously reported that, after four months of training, Estonian troops carried out their first live-fire exercises using the country’s own HIMARS rocket systems.
The wartime structure of the Estonian Defense Forces includes more than 43,000 positions. About 4,200 are assigned to active-duty personnel, while the rest are reservists and members of the Estonian Defense League (Kaitseliit).
As of 2026, the Estonian Division forms the core of the land component of the Estonian Defense Forces. It is the country’s largest land formation, reports directly to the Commander of the Defense Forces, and is integrated into NATO’s command structure.
The division includes the 1st and 2nd Infantry Brigades, a headquarters and signals battalion, an ISTAR reconnaissance battalion, and artillery, engineering, and logistics battalions.
The division’s main maneuver unit remains the 1st Infantry Brigade. It comprises the Scouts Battalion, the Kalev and Viru infantry battalions, an air defense battalion, a combat support battalion, headquarters and signals companies, and an anti-tank company.
The brigade also trains conscripts, who are later transferred to the reserve.
The 2nd Infantry Brigade is primarily responsible for the southeastern part of the country. In peacetime, it consists of a headquarters in Tartu, the Kuperjanov Battalion in Võru, a combat support battalion, and a support and communications company. In wartime, the brigade is expanded with reserve units.
In addition to the division, the Estonian Defense Forces include the Cyber Command, Support Command, Military Police, Special Operations Forces, and other units.

articles.title: Russia Ordered MZKT Chassis, Presumably for Pechora-2M Systems
articles.body:
The Minsk Wheeled Tractor Plant (MZKT) has signed a contract with the Moscow-based JSC Defense Systems to supply 30 specialized wheeled chassis.
This is evidenced by documents obtained by the Belarusian association BELPOL.
Under the terms of the agreement, the Russian customer is to receive 20 MZKT-8021-021 chassis, as well as five units each of the MZKT-8022-021 and MZKT-80211-021 models.
The contract is long-term and provides for equipment delivery through 2029.
The MZKT-8021/8022 series of specialized chassis was developed specifically to house components of the Pechora-2M air defense missile system.
In addition, these wheeled platforms also mount other air defense systems and radar stations.
The Russian joint-stock company Defense Systems specializes in developing, modernizing, and serially producing air defense and electronic warfare systems.
The company’s main and best-known project is the extensive modernization of Soviet short- and medium-range air defense systems of the Pechora series to the Pechora-2M and Pechora-2K standards, supplied to both the Russian Armed Forces and for export.
The size of the order indicates Russia’s intention to use Pechora-2M systems or air defense systems compatible with them.
Against the backdrop of a shortage of air defense capabilities, a return to Soviet-era systems is a practical step due to the availability of significant stockpiles of corresponding ammunition.
The system is a major upgrade of the S-125M air defense system and is designed to engage air targets at ranges from 3.5 to 32 km and at altitudes from 20 meters to 20 km.
In 2024, Belarus was to supply Russia with 18 MZKT-7930-312 chassis for producing Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft gun-missile systems.

articles.title: Lithuania proposes special status for Ukrainian ammunition project
articles.body:
A project by Baltic Metal Foundry, the Lithuanian subsidiary of Ukrainian defence company Dnipro Electromechanical Plant (DEMZ), to manufacture ammunition and munitions components in Lithuania is being proposed for special status.
The Economy and Innovation Ministry has drafted a government resolution that would designate the project as meeting urgent state security and defence needs. The status would allow the company to benefit from special investment and business conditions beyond those provided under Lithuania’s Investment Law.
The ministry said the decision would contribute to improving the business environment and increasing investment.
Baltic Metal Foundry signed an investment agreement with the ministry in mid-August. Under the agreement, the company plans to manufacture ammunition and munitions components in Alytus and the Prienai district, with the project expected to create up to 450 jobs.
The value of the investment was not disclosed when the agreement was signed. Alytus Mayor Nerijus Cesiulis said at the time that the Ukrainian company planned to invest tens of millions of euros in the town.
Lithuania’s list of major investment projects shows that the company has committed to investing at least 93.3 million euros in the project.
An ammunition assembly plant is planned for the Prienai district, while existing infrastructure at the Alytus industrial park will be used to manufacture metal munitions components.
Construction of the plant near Balbieriškis was expected to begin this autumn, with production scheduled to start late next year or in the autumn of 2027. The facility is planned on a 30.6-hectare site in the village of Ąžuolai.
The company has said its products will meet NATO standards. Its primary market will be the Ukrainian armed forces, while production will also serve the defence needs of allied countries.
DEMZ is a major supplier of defence products to Ukraine’s military. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the company shifted its operations from civilian to military production. It has branches across Ukraine and employs about 4,000 people.
Baltic Metal Foundry was registered in Vilnius just over a year ago and currently has one employee, according to Lithuania’s State Social Insurance Fund, Sodra.
Data from the Centre of Registers shows that the company’s beneficiaries include two Polish citizens and one Ukrainian citizen.

articles.title: Rubio Heads To NATO Allies As Russian Threat, Middle East War Shape Agenda
articles.body:
WASHINGTON -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is heading to Iceland, Greece, and Portugal on October 5-8 for talks on security, defense, energy, economic cooperation, and technology as NATO allies face growing security concerns over Russia’s military activity and continued Middle East instability.
Rubio will begin in Reykjavik, where he is expected to discuss Arctic security and economic cooperation with Icelandic officials.
He will then travel to Athens for the sixth US-Greece Strategic Dialogue, with defense cooperation, energy, regional security, Ukraine, and the Middle East on the agenda.
In Lisbon, his talks will focus on defense, economic development, and technology cooperation, according to the State Department.
The three stops include different areas of US cooperation with NATO allies, from Iceland’s role in North Atlantic and Arctic security to Greece’s position in the Eastern Mediterranean and Portugal’s long-standing importance to US military operations in the Atlantic.
Iceland: Security And The Arctic
Iceland has no standing army but has long cooperated with the US and NATO on security because of its location in the North Atlantic.
Two former US ambassadors to Iceland -- who spoke on the condition of anonymity -- told RFE/RL that Rubio should expect Reykjavik to be receptive to further security cooperation, while also listening to the concerns of a country that places a high value on its independence.
“Icelanders are a fiercely independent people,” one ambassador said, adding that there has been continued US-Icelandic security cooperation since Russia’s invasion of Crimea in 2014.
Separately, Robert Gerber, a former US diplomat who served at the US Embassy in Iceland, said Rubio's visit could follow up on commitments discussed at a September meeting of Arctic countries on the margins of the UN General Assembly.
Those discussions included commitments by Arctic partners to take greater responsibility for their own security and the protection of critical infrastructure.
Gerber also pointed to his own experience in Iceland to illustrate the security concerns facing the country.
“When I was in Iceland on a regular basis, Russian aircraft or bombers or whatever would fly toward Iceland, do a loop of the island, and then fly back just to see how fast NATO planes would scramble,” Gerber told RFE/RL.
“The threat is real there, and it's been there for a long time,” Gerber said, adding that submarine warfare in the region is also a continuing concern.
Iceland's contribution to NATO differs from that of larger allies, Gerber said. The country hosts Keflavik Air Base, has contributed to Ukraine, and provides maritime and search-and-rescue capabilities through its Coast Guard.
Gerber said the protection of undersea telecommunications cables linking North America and Europe could also be an area for greater cooperation.
Russians In The Arctic
“Those obviously need to be hardened and protected because the Russians are up to all kinds of things in the Arctic,” he said. Iceland's Coast Guard, including its ships and helicopters, could also be important in an Arctic crisis, he added.
Gerber said he did not expect Rubio to persuade Iceland to make a major change in its defense spending. “Iceland's economy is relatively small,” Gerber said, adding that the country's approach to security is also shaped by its independent political outlook.
Eric Green, a former White House National Security Council official who also served as deputy chief of mission in Iceland, said Icelandic officials would also be looking for reassurance from Washington.
“It’s positive that Secretary Rubio is visiting NATO countries,” Green told RFE/RL, adding that Icelandic officials would want reassurance that Washington was no longer interested in making claims on Greenland based on what he called “spurious accusations.”
Green also said Iceland, a strong supporter of Ukraine, would welcome indications that Washington intends to do more to help Ukraine and Europe as Russia continues its war.
The Arctic has also become a focus of competition as melting ice opens new maritime routes and increases interest in the region's resources.
The former ambassador said Russia has strengthened its military presence along its Arctic coast, while China has sought to expand its presence through port, research and other initiatives in Iceland.
Greece: Defense, Energy, Regional Security
In Athens, Rubio will lead the US delegation at the sixth US-Greece Strategic Dialogue on October 6-7.
The dialogue, launched in 2018, provides a framework for cooperation on defense, energy, and other issues. The talks are expected to include the facilities and support Greece provides under the Mutual Defense Cooperation Agreement, as well as developments in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Geoffrey Pyatt, a former assistant secretary of state for energy resources and former US ambassador to Greece and Ukraine, said the dialogue was established as a way to advance bilateral cooperation independently of other regional relationships.
“When we created the Strategic Dialogue during my tenure as ambassador, the whole idea was to create a forum to advance the strong agenda of bilateral cooperation topics independent of any other regional relationships,” Pyatt told RFE/RL.
He said military cooperation, energy opportunities, and people-to-people ties, including education and investment, have remained consistent across Republican and Democratic administrations.
Pyatt also pointed to Greece's commitment to its European and transatlantic relationships. “Greece remains strongly committed to its European identity including the firm commitment to the transatlantic relationship,” he said.
Rubio's final stop will be Lisbon, where the State Department says he will discuss defense, economic development and technology cooperation with the country’s leadership.
Portugal's role in US security cooperation includes the Azores, where Lajes Air Base has long provided an important logistical and refueling location for US military operations in the Atlantic.

articles.title: Russian drones strike cargo ship in Black Sea, kill captain, Zelensky says
articles.body:
A cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast on Oct. 5 after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.
At the time of the attack, the ship was sailing outside Romania's territorial waters but within the country's exclusive economic zone, about 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers) from the Romanian coast and roughly 9 nautical miles (16.6 kilometers) southeast of the Pescarus offshore oil platform operated by OMV Petrom, according to Romanian media outlet Digi24.ro. First reports had placed the incident near the Neptun Deep gas development.
"Ukraine has repeatedly proposed concrete steps to de-escalate and guarantee security in the Black Sea. There have also been corresponding proposals from third countries," Zelensky said.
"But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian ships instead of normal navigation. Pressure is needed to restore global food security. And everyone who is truly interested in this should help."
Romania's Interior Ministry later said 11 crew members had been rescued. The vessel was sinking, while injured survivors were evacuated for emergency medical treatment. Romanian authorities had not provided details about the cause of the fire.
The incident is the latest in a string of Russian attacks that has crippled civilian and commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
Ukraine's maritime corridor, opened in 2023 after Russia withdrew from the U.N.-backed grain deal, has been largely closed again after a spate of Russian attacks, both on port infrastructure and ships themselves, over summer 2026.
The International Maritime Organization has warned that the war poses a "serious and immediate threat" to crews and vessels operating in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
The latest incident comes two days after a Russian strike on a Liberian-flagged cargo ship in Ukraine's Odesa region killed one person and injured three, according to Ukrainian port authorities cited by Reuters.

articles.title: Cocaine Boatmen Are Being Blown Up By US Airstrikes, But The Drugs Keep Flowing From Colombia
articles.body:
That has left the work of identifying these men to local communities and journalists, such as a consortium led by the Latin American investigative outlet CLIP that was able to collect the names, or at least some information, about 19 men killed between September 2 and May 5.
When reached for comment, the U.S. Southern Command declined to discuss how they identify targets, but said that “every narco-terrorist neutralized” as part of the campaign “was an affiliated member of a Designated Terrorist Organization, actively transporting illicit material along known trafficking routes in international waters.” 
In their update on Operation Southern Spear one year in, U.S. officials were less bullish than their president, but said the campaign had driven a 60 percent reduction in illicit maritime activity in the Eastern Caribbean region that includes La Guajira. They also touted a 65 percent reduction in the Western Caribbean and a nearly 50 percent reduction in key areas of the Eastern Pacific.
The Trump administration does not disclose how it measures success, but a July report issued by the Washington Office on Latin America, a rights advocacy group, noted that available evidence suggested the military campaign was having little to no impact on the supply of cocaine reaching the U.S. 
Catalina Niño, a project coordinator at the local branch of the German pro-democracy non-profit Friedrich Ebert Stiftung, noted that “there is nothing to indicate that the strategy is achieving its supposed objective.”
“There is no evidence that the strategy works, not even in terms of physical proof, because destroying the boats leaves no evidence behind. There are no individuals to prosecute, and there is no verifiable evidence that there were drugs on those boats in the first place,” she said. “It is impossible to obtain evidence in this regard.”
When reached for comment, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said that “all of these decisive strikes have been against designated narcoterrorists bringing deadly poison to our shores, and the President will continue to use every element of American power to stop drugs from flooding into our country and to bring those responsible to justice.”
Colombia’s presidency did not respond to requests to comment. The country’s deputy ombudsman, Paula Aponte, said in a statement that her office has sought further information from other state agencies on the Colombian nationals believed to have died in the attacks, but with little success. 
Searching for a Body 
Down one dusty dirt road in Riohacha sits a single-story brick home where a grief-stricken Wayúu family has been waiting for a boatman to return since May. The family, who lives without running water, has traveled across the peninsula to look for his corpse. They also constantly scan social media, where graphic videos of casualties from decimated boats circulate.
“He hasn’t appeared. They have asked about him even in the Dominican Republic,” said a distraught woman who answered the door to the family’s home and identified herself as a neighbor.
The woman explained that without a body, the man’s mother refuses to accept his death. 
But many believe the moment his life ended was captured in the video accompanying a Southern Command press release announcing a May 4 missile strike on a vessel “operated by Designated Terrorist Organizations” in the Caribbean Sea.
“Two male narco-terrorists were killed during this action,” the press release declared. 
After that announcement, word quickly spread in La Guajira that the men might be from the Wayúu community that has inhabited this desert for hundreds of years.

articles.title: ARX and Roboneers deepen Ukraine drone partnership
articles.body:
German defence technology company ARX Robotics and Ukrainian firm Roboneers have agreed a wider partnership covering unmanned ground systems, including technical integration and joint development work for Ukrainian and other European forces, according to ARX Robotics.
The agreement was signed in Kyiv during a German state visit to Ukraine, in the presence of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Under the partnership, the two companies plan to deepen the integration of their respective unmanned systems and continue joint development work around ground robotics for military use. Both companies are already supplying uncrewed ground vehicles to the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
The latest agreement follows an earlier deal reached in June 2026 to establish ARX Industries, a production joint venture intended to manufacture the Rys Pro unmanned ground vehicle in Ukraine and Germany.
The Rys Pro is developed by Roboneers, which produces a range of Ukrainian unmanned ground and aerial systems alongside software and remote weapon technologies. The company says its platforms are used for roles including frontline logistics, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance and combat support.
ARX Robotics, meanwhile, develops its Gereon family of unmanned ground vehicles and the Mithra OS software platform, which is designed to provide autonomous and digital functions across military land systems.
According to a news update from ARX Robotics, company chief executive Marc Wietfeld said: “Software-defined unmanned defense solutions are key for landforces on a modern battlefield where every action can be seen by the enemy. Together with Roboneers we provide the Ukrainian forces with a robust but smart UGV fleet at scale and at the same time ensure that the lessons learnt from the battlefield are incorporated into the landsystems development of other western armies.”
The companies are positioning the partnership around both immediate Ukrainian requirements and the wider development of autonomous land systems for European armed forces. ARX said feedback from systems operating in Ukraine would be incorporated into future land-platform development, allowing lessons from frontline use to influence software, vehicle design and operating concepts elsewhere.
The Ukrainian government estimates that national demand for unmanned ground systems could reach 50,000 units during 2026, according to the company.
ARX also states that its Gereon vehicles currently represent the largest fleet of Western-built unmanned ground systems operating in Ukraine. The use of UGVs has expanded during the war as Ukrainian forces have increasingly used unmanned platforms to move supplies, evacuate casualties, conduct reconnaissance and support combat activity while reducing the need to expose personnel to direct fire.
For manufacturers, the scale and pace of operations in Ukraine has also created demand for systems that can be produced in quantity, repaired quickly and adapted through software or modular payloads as battlefield requirements change. ARX has been expanding its industrial capacity alongside the operational partnership. The company has recently worked with German industrial firms including Deutz as it seeks to increase production of unmanned ground vehicles. The Roboneers partnership adds a Ukrainian manufacturing and development component to that effort through the previously announced ARX Industries joint venture.
Roboneers says its Rys Pro UGV and Saber remote weapon station have been deployed across units of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, with its systems collectively used during more than 15,000 frontline missions since 2014. ARX Robotics was founded in 2022 and currently employs around 300 people across Munich, Berlin, London and Kyiv. Its work is centred on autonomous ground platforms and software intended to add digital and autonomous functions to both new and existing military vehicles.
Roboneers describes its own approach as a multi-domain robotic ecosystem spanning unmanned ground vehicles, unmanned aerial systems and associated software, with development and manufacturing conducted in Ukraine. The latest agreement expands an existing relationship between the two companies from production of individual systems towards closer technical integration, joint development and a broader approach to unmanned land warfare.
