articles.title: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers from base
articles.body:
Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers that had been stationed at the Gloucestershire base amid security concerns about a possible threat from Iran.
The prime minister’s official spokesperson, speaking during a scheduled briefing, said “yes” when asked if the military site was safe – contrasting with the concern showed by the US military during the hasty redeployment the day before.
Pointing to comments made last week by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the official said there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”, highlighting protection of the airbase.
Aircraft trackers reported that an entire squadron of 12 B-1 bombers based at Fairford had redeployed from the British base to the US on Sunday, a rapid movement that was confirmed by the Pentagon on Sunday evening.
US officials told the New York Times that commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the site. Some of the bombers left so quickly that refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled to support their flights to the US.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said on Monday military deployments were normal and tried to downplay any discrepancies with the UK. He said the US was confident in the security of all its bases and “with the Brits, we’ve worked very closely a long time, including on this investigation, and they couldn’t be more cooperative”.
Downing Street’s comments were the first made by British authorities in the light of the US withdrawal. No comment was made by the Ministry of Defence or Gloucestershire police when asked if there was any additional threat to residents near the base. Other UK officials indicated they had not been briefed on US thinking.
RAF Fairford has already been on high alert for several weeks amid a heightened American concern that Tehran could try to instigate an attack on the base, which had been used for US air force bombing runs against Iran earlier this year. In July, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said the base was a legitimate military target.
It is unclear what level of threat Iran could pose to a military base in the heart of the UK, though Iran has destroyed US planes on the tarmac during fighting earlier this year. Missiles fired from Iran may be able to reach the UK but would likely be shot down first; a drone attack would be a high-risk operation close to the base.
Developments in the UK have not so far matched the apparent level of the US warnings. At the end of September five men from London driving white vans to Whelford, a village by the base, were arrested in the small hours on suspicion of carrying explosives.
No explosive devices were found in the search, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. All five were released on police bail a day later, raising questions about what they had been doing.
Afterwards, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was “surprised” the five men had been allowed out on bail. “We know everything about them, we would not have released them,” he said.
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has been more muted. Last week he said there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, but developments in the British investigation, led by counter-terror police, have been limited.
A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested in Westminster, London, on Thursday on suspicion of preparing acts of terrorism, but he was also released on police bail on Saturday. Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the events in Gloucestershire were continuing, counter-terror police added.

articles.title: External affairs minister S Jaishankar says US has chosen to become 'lonelier power'
articles.body:
External affairs minister S Jaishankar addresses the 62nd Munich Security Conference in New Delhi
NEW DELHI: Foreign minister S Jaishankar said US had deliberately chosen to become a "lonelier power", while reiterating Russia's longstanding support for India."At a time when much of the world preferred backing a military regime next to us (Pakistan), Russia was a country with which our relations were very good, and we are shaped in many ways by that legacy," he said at Munich Leaders Meeting here.He said India's Russia-Ukraine conflict approach had moved beyond just the advocacy of dialogue, suggesting India might now be looking to actively mediate.
World today is marked by America’s radical repositioning and China’s rise, says Jaishankar
Both Moscow and Kyiv have said recently that India had come up with ideas and proposals to bring an end to the war. Unlike China and others that have looked to mediate, India had so far supported global peace efforts — advocating dialogue between the parties — but had not come up its own proposal, reflecting its emphasis on bilateral resolution of disputes.Offering a teaser on India’s proposal, Jaishankar said India is looking to address some immediate concerns that both Russia and Ukraine have on “grain exports, energy exports, non-attack possibilities”.“We would like to see an end to this conflict. This will require dialogue and diplomacy. We have been advocating it for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy. We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard.
We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue,” said the minister, speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting here.Jaishankar had said during his visit to Ukraine last month — shortly after PM Narendra Modi’s message to Russian President Vladimir Putin to stop the “endless war” — that India was discussing ideas that could be developed for cessation of hostilities.
On Friday, while Putin announced Modi had very good ideas for peace, Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said India had come up with the “broadest” peace proposal out of the four that it had received from other countries, including the US.This shift in India’s position seems driven by direct domestic fallout of the conflict, whether it’s commercial shipping disruptions in Black Sea or an intense blowback from US over India’s continued purchase of Russian crude.On US, Jaishankar said the world today was marked by a radical repositioning of the US, and also the rise of China.“The current system was significantly underwritten by the United States. That underwriting is diluting.” He underlined that the sharp competition between US and China was not limited to them alone. “It has led to weaponisation of any leverage that any country has. ”

articles.title: Iran serious about diplomacy, defence
articles.body:
Speaking Sunday morning to ambassadors and heads of diplomatic missions and international organisation offices resident in Tehran, Araghchi outlined Iran's positions on regional developments and gave a report on the diplomatic activities of the delegation sent to the 81st UN General Assembly.
He pointed to Iran's influential and powerful presence at the General Assembly and detailed the main actions taken during the New York visit, including consultations with presidents and foreign ministers of more than 60 countries and senior officials of regional and international organisations, as well as talks with think tanks and media.
Araghchi stressed Iran's determination to protect its national rights and interests, and explained Iran's proposed initiative for restoring security to the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. He said the world clearly witnessed Iran's goodwill and continuous seriousness in using diplomacy to prevent escalation.
"It became clear to everyone at this assembly that the Islamic Republic of Iran is serious about diplomacy, just as it is serious and determined in defending itself," Araghchi said.
Explaining Iran's principled position on US excessive demands, he said: "If the enemies again choose the path of military confrontation and war, Iran's response will be much firmer and more decisive than before."
Araghchi condemned what he called the contemptible behaviour of US officials towards the Iranian delegation, including the claim that its members were expelled. He said the delegation's entry and exit took place according to the previously announced schedule. Despite this, US officials, to compensate for their failure to portray Iran as isolated, resorted to lies and claimed the delegation was expelled, which is on the one hand a clear admission of America's violation of its international obligations as host of the United Nations, and on the other shows US officials' anger at Iran's influential presence at the most important international event.
The foreign minister also referred to meetings with neighbouring countries, including Persian Gulf states, and stressed Iran's decision to continue building confidence among regional countries based on the principle of good neighbourliness, in order to strengthen cooperation and coordination to enhance regional peace and security.
Referring to meetings with European parties, he stressed that Iran has conveyed its positions on the need for European countries to adopt a responsible and independent approach to West Asian issues. He cited repeated admissions by NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte about extensive direct European participation in illegal and aggressive US and Israeli attacks on Iran, and demanded that European countries be held accountable for their role in designing and carrying out the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran.
Condemning US "inhumane and illegal" sanctions against Iran, Araghchi stressed that sanctions, pressure and threats cannot shake the Iranian nation's determination to defend its rights and dignity.
In his speech, Araghchi thanked the diplomats for arranging his and the president's meetings in New York. "I met with 42 foreign ministers in New York. The president met with almost 10 heads of state, and all of this was thanks to the efforts and coordination you made."
He said Iran's presence in New York this year was very strong and effective. In addition to the many meetings, there were many interviews, the president's speech at the General Assembly and other speeches Araghchi gave at side events, and meetings with thinkers, political elites and intellectuals in New York. Most important, he said, was the plan Iran presented this year to resolve existing disputes and the ongoing war between Iran and America, known as the seven-day plan, under which the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened within seven days if accepted.
Iran's presence at this year's General Assembly was very effective and active. The political atmosphere in New York this year was affected by Iran's plan and Iran's very broad presence, and it became clear to everyone that Iran remains serious about diplomacy and finding a peaceful solution.
"As we are serious in defending ourselves, we are firm and serious in both defending ourselves and advancing diplomacy. If our enemies again take the path of military confrontation, they will receive a firmer response than before, and we will defend ourselves more strongly than before. On the other hand, if they seek diplomatic paths, we remain ready to reach a just and honourable solution through diplomacy to end this war."
Araghchi said Iran explained its positions clearly. The level of interest from different countries in meeting Iran, learning its views and understanding its plan was very significant. "The perception some in America may have had that they could turn Iran into an isolated country was completely defeated, and Iran played its role in New York as a powerful and respected country in the international community, showing that it still has logical positions and has a solution both for war and for peace."
He said the US claim that it expelled the Iranian delegation, regardless of its truth, is noteworthy because Iran went to New York and returned according to its own pre-set schedule. "This claim by the American side is truly strange. On the one hand, they admit they acted contrary to their obligations as host of the United Nations and are not a worthy host for the organisation, and on the other, they showed how angry they are at the presence of the Iranian delegation in America, exactly as if the host of the Olympics, when its team loses, expels the athletes of another team. This behaviour is just as childish and contemptible."
Araghchi said Iran's diplomats had a brilliant presence at the General Assembly. "We were present in all arenas, conveyed the voice of the Iranian people to the world, and delivered the message of the Iranian people for peace and logical and peaceful solutions.
We explained our conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz clearly to everyone. All these conditions are consistent with the commitments the United States must accept."
He said meetings with neighbouring countries, especially Persian Gulf states, were very effective, respectful and friendly. "We have begun a new path to build trust between neighbouring countries and the Islamic Republic of Iran, and especially in the Persian Gulf, we are traversing this path well."
"Our brothers and sisters in the Persian Gulf are accompanying us on this path, and a shared will has formed to create peace, stability and security in the Persian Gulf region with the participation of the region's own countries, which is now being seriously pursued."
He said he also had many meetings with European countries. "You are all aware that our dialogue with European countries is very frank, and we hope European countries will reconsider their approach towards the Islamic Republic of Iran."
Araghchi said the NATO secretary-general's admission of European participation in the US war against Iran was a heavy admission. "He clearly said that more than 5,000 American warplanes flew from bases in Europe to attack Iran, and we are still waiting for European countries to answer why they effectively participated in this war against Iran. European countries must reconsider their approach towards Iran."
He said Iran hopes America will choose the path of wisdom and rationality, but if it again moves toward military solutions, "we are more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves. If they choose the path of diplomacy, we remain ready."
"America has lost both in war and in diplomacy in the past. Testing the path of sanctions and new sanctions will bring them no benefit. There is no military solution and no solution based on more sanctions; only a solution based on negotiation, justice, fairness and diplomatic dignity can be effective and find a final solution to end this war and the illegal and unjust aggression that has been launched against the Islamic Republic of Iran."
MNA

articles.title: Heritage is identity: Iranian archaeologist exposes scale of war destruction to historic sites
articles.body:
Heritage is identity: Iranian archaeologist exposes scale of war destruction to historic sites
TEHRAN – An Iranian archaeologist, Sonia Shidrang, highlighted in a global webinar hosted by the International Committee on Archaeological Heritage Management (ICAHM), a scientific committee under ICOMOS, that the 40-day war with the United States and the Israeli regime left 149 historical sites across 20 provinces damaged, and that Iran's cultural heritage now demands a response grounded in international law, rigorous documentation, and a concrete protection plan.
The ICAHM Webinars 2026 took place on Sep. 30, chaired by Matt Whincop, ICAHM Secretary General, and focused on the theme "From Vulnerability to Resilience: Protecting Cultural Heritage from Natural and Anthropogenic Disasters."
The program featured two speakers addressing heritage protection from complementary angles. Professor Hatice Pamir from the Department of Archaeology of Mustafa Kemal University, Turkey, presented "Earthquakes and the Archaeological Heritage of Antioch on the Banks of the Orontes River: Lessons Learnt from Fieldwork," focusing on seismic threats to archaeological sites.
Shidrang followed with "Iranian Cultural Heritage Under Fire: Documentation, Risk, and a Plan for Protection," examining conflict-related risks and strategies for safeguarding heritage. Together, the talks spanned both natural and human-induced disasters, reflecting the webinar's central concern with building resilience for cultural heritage.
Shidrang, a faculty member at Shahid Beheshti University, opened with a reminder that heritage is not merely about ancient monuments. "It is about identity. It is about memory. It is about the shared story of humanity," she said, adding that war's direct and indirect effects on tangible and intangible cultural heritage are irreversible and irreparable.
According to the Iranian Ministry of Cultural Heritage, the joint US-Israeli military campaign that began on February 28, 2026, severely damaged districts, houses, prominent buildings, museums, and cultural sites. The Ministry has called the destruction "a clear violation of international law" and "a threat against the historical memory of humanity."
Among the damaged sites are five UNESCO World Heritage properties: the Golestan Palace in Tehran, the Naqsh-e Jahan Square complex and Imam Mosque in Isfahan, and the Trans-Iranian Railway, which was struck at five stations on the final night of the conflict.
Shidrang anchored her presentation in the 1954 Hague Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in the Event of Armed Conflict, noting that Iran is a State Party to the Convention and its Protocols. She cited Article 3, which requires states to prepare in peacetime to safeguard cultural property, and said the Ministry moved valuable artifacts to secure storage and installed protective coverings before and during the war. She also pointed to Article 4(1), which obligates parties to refrain from any act of hostility directed against cultural property; Article 6, which provides for the Blue Shield emblem to mark protected sites; Article 7, which requires respect for cultural property to be integrated into military regulations; and the 1999 Second Protocol, which establishes individual criminal responsibility for violations. Iran, she noted, installed Blue Shield markers on museums and historic buildings. "The distinctive emblem has legal force under Article 6 only if parties are aware of it and choose to respect it," she said.
The scale of the destruction, according to the Ministry's latest estimates by early summer, included five UNESCO World Heritage sites, seven historical fabrics, and 54 museums damaged to varying degrees. 74 sites were damaged by blast waves, 42 by strikes on their buffer zones, and 33 by direct strikes on their premises. Tehran Province ranks first with 83 damaged sites, nearly half of the total; of these, 36 are inscribed on the National Heritage List, and six were completely destroyed, including the Rafi Nia Synagogue and the Pasteur Institute. Isfahan Province ranks second with 27 sites, followed by Kurdistan with 13, Khuzestan with 12, Kermanshah with five, Lorestan with four, Qom with three, and other provinces with 15. The financial estimate of damage, initially calculated at approximately €27.08 billion, has now risen to €36.10 billion, with more than €7.22 billion of that representing damage to the Golestan and Sa'dabad Palace complexes alone.
The Golestan Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage site, was severely damaged on March 1, 2026, when an Israeli missile struck a nearby building in the Grand Bazaar. The Shams-ol-Emareh structure was hit, and the head of the Marble Throne statue was severed. The Tehran Grand Bazaar was also severely damaged. The Sa'dabad Palace complex was hit by five bunker-buster bombs on March 16, 2026, collapsing roofs and walls across three palaces, shattering 6,000 square meters of glass, and causing structural failure at the Omidvar Brothers Museum.
Despite the destruction, Iran was not passive. On the first day of the war, the National Museum of Iran transferred all movable objects from its exhibition halls to secure storage and then protected large, immovable objects in place. Fire-resistant thermal insulation was wrapped around artifacts, sandbag walls were erected, and metal framing reinforced them against shrapnel and heat.
Shidrang said that, according to the Iranian Ministry of Cultural Heritage, emergency protection is now complete, with buildings prioritized by age and structural strength. As of this summer, emergency restoration had been completed at 10 sites, including the Golestan Palace, Sa'dabad Palace, the Glassware Museum, and the Museum of Contemporary Art, along with two buildings in West Azerbaijan and several sites in Isfahan, Zanjan, and Qom. Restoration is underway at 21 sites, including the Museum of Decorative Arts and Chehel Sotoun Palace in Isfahan and the Khosrowabad and Moshir Mansions in Kurdistan. Documentation for structural reinforcement of the Blue Dome of Maragheh has been completed, documentation of Baba Taher's Tomb in Hamadan is in progress, and debris-clearing of the Falak al-Aflak buffer zone in Lorestan has been completed by military institutions.
The Secretary-General of the Iranian National Commission for UNESCO has reported the compilation of several thousand pages of documentation concerning damage sustained by the nation's educational and cultural infrastructure and cultural heritage during the recent wars. He further stated that, through UNESCO's follow-up, a number of countries—including Japan and South Korea—have signaled their readiness to contribute to the reconstruction of Iran's cultural heritage, with some €2.5 million in assistance having been pledged.
Shidrang also pointed to reports showing that, from the first days, the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, in cooperation with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, initiated extensive consultations and correspondence with international bodies, issuing six statements and nine letters to organizations including UNESCO, the International Council of Museums (ICOM), ICOMOS, and the World Tourism Organization. UNESCO, ICOMOS, and ICOM were informed of the details of the damage and condemned the attacks. ICOMOS condemned the destruction "whether intentional or incidental" and recalled that cultural heritage must not be considered a target, while ICOM called on all parties to comply with their obligations under the 1954 Hague Convention and its Protocols. Iran has cited international legal instruments including the 1954 Hague Convention, the 1972 World Heritage Convention, the 2003 Intangible Heritage Convention, UN Security Council Resolution 2347, and legal mechanisms related to the Hague Tribunal. However, despite these efforts, no adequate response was given to Iran's requests for international assistance for reconstruction.
Based on the 1954 Hague Convention and the current situation, Dr. Shidrang proposed a five-point protection plan. The first point calls for accelerating Blue Shield implementation and enforcement, accompanied by formal notification to all parties through UNESCO and the 1954 Hague Convention Secretariat, because the distinctive emblem has legal force under Article 6 only if parties are aware of it and choose to respect it. The second calls for safe haven and evacuation protocols, extending protective covering, sandbagging, and structural reinforcement to immovable heritage where possible and invoking the International Register of Cultural Property under Special Protection under Article 8 for the most significant sites. The third calls for a no-strike list and military coordination, formalizing UNESCO-provided coordinates into a no-strike list communicated through military channels, with Article 7 specialist personnel embedded in command structures to advise on cultural property protection and with the "military necessity" exception interpreted narrowly and documented transparently. The fourth calls for emergency funding and technical support, with UNESCO, ICOMOS, ICCROM, and the Blue Shield establishing a joint emergency fund for immediate stabilization, documentation, and conservation—not as a matter of politics, she said, but to fulfill the obligation to protect the cultural heritage of all humanity. The fifth calls for legal accountability and monitoring, documenting the damage for future legal proceedings before the International Criminal Court, the International Court of Justice, or other mechanisms, and establishing a standing monitoring mechanism—perhaps a joint UNESCO-ICOMOS-ICOM task force—to receive, verify, and publish reports on cultural heritage damage in the conflict zone.
The session, chaired by ICAHM Secretary General Matt Whincop, concluded with an exchange regarding the future of Iranian heritage management within the international arena. As the international community continues to grapple with the protection of the world’s shared past, the collaborative efforts exemplified by the webinar highlighted the vital necessity of fostering institutional partnerships.
AM

articles.title: Russian Paratroopers Airdrop Kurier UGV from an Il-76 for the First Time During Center-2026 Exercises
articles.body:
During the Center-2026 strategic command-and-staff exercises, Russian paratroopers airdropped the Kurier ground-based robotic complex from an Ilyushin Il-76 military transport aircraft for the first time.
The Russian Ministry of Defense published a video of the airdrop.
The system was dropped from about 600 meters on a P-7 parachute platform.
The operators of these systems had previously landed in the mission area, after which they took control of the robotic vehicles.
According to the exercise scenario, the robots were to operate behind enemy lines.
They were intended to provide fire support for assault units, deliver ammunition and supplies, evacuate the wounded, and destroy road infrastructure.
During one exercise, the Kurier was deployed to provide fire support for an assault group. A 7.62-mm machine gun was mounted on the system. According to a Russian operator, after landing, the robot requires about three to five minutes to prepare for the mission.
Separately, during the exercises, reconnaissance teams parachuted from an An-26 aircraft at an altitude of 6,000 meters.
The troops used special Stayer parachute systems equipped with oxygen apparatus. After jumping, they glided more than 17 km and landed behind enemy lines.
In addition to Kurier, the Omich-2 and Bogomol-7V ground-based robotic systems also participated in the exercises.
Militarnyi previously reported that in the Chelyabinsk region, the Russians conducted exercises to repel external aggression and establish a security zone on the territory of a Central Asian country.
After repelling the main assault in the South Ural direction, the troops went on the offensive to liberate the occupied territory and establish a security zone in the adjacent territory.
UGV Kurier is a Russian multi-purpose ground robot on a tracked chassis with remote control. Its design allows for the installation of various equipment and weapons depending on the mission.
According to publicly available data, the base version measures about 1.4 × 1.2 × 0.58 m, weighs up to 250 kg, and can reach speeds up to 35 km/h. The control range is 3 to 10 km, and the operational endurance is up to 72 hours.
The Kurier delivers ammunition, food, and other cargo; evacuates the wounded; conducts reconnaissance; and lays mines. For combat missions, the robot is equipped with various weapons, including a 7.62-mm PKTM machine gun, 12.7-mm NSVT or Kord machine guns, and AGS-17 and AGS-30 automatic grenade launchers. In 2025, the Ignis laser system was also tested on the Kurier platform to destroy mines at distances up to 150 m.

articles.title: Ukraine has put more than 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity out of action
articles.body:
Ukraine has put more than 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity out of action
Ukrainian long-range operations have put more than 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity out of action.
Source: Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara, quoted by the Defence Ministry
Quote: "Intelligence and analysts from the General Staff and the Defence Ministry have assessed the impact of the recent long-range strikes by the defence forces. More than half of the enemy's capacity has been put out of action. This is the result of carefully planned, systematic and consistent actions aimed at bleeding the Russian war machine dry and destroying its military and economic potential."
Details: Khmara said that the Moscow, Yaroslavl, Kinef, Ust-Luga, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, Syzran and other oil refineries have been hit recently.
Quote: "Fifty-one per cent of oil refining capacity being hit is a significant blow to the enemy's economy, its ability to wage aggression and supply its troop deployments. Our deep strikes continue to take the war onto Russian territory."
Details: As Khmara noted, one of the Defence Ministry's priorities is long-range attack drones, which make it possible to strike targets deep inside Russia.
"We have tripled production and procurement this year. This is not the limit. We will continue to scale up our deep-strike capabilities," the statement said.

articles.title: Germany risks being drawn into ‘violent conflict’ with Russia, spy chief warns
articles.body:
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz, right, and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visit the war-damaged Ukrainian Academy of Science in Kyiv on Oct. 4, 2026. | Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — Germany's foreign intelligence chief warned Monday of the rising risk of a direct clash with Russia as the Kremlin escalates its “shadow war” on Berlin and hits Ukraine with increasing brutality.
“Germany is in danger of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia,” Martin Jäger, the head of the German’s foreign intelligence agency, or BND, told parliamentarians, citing what he called Russia’s attempted attack on a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig Airport in August as an example. “Germany has become a major obstacle to Russia’s hegemonic power projection in Europe and, as a result, a primary target of Russian actions.”
Jäger also warned that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is entering its most dangerous phase yet as President Vladimir Putin faces growing domestic pressure to show military progress with the war entering its fifth winter.
Advertisement
“Russia is determined to bring Ukraine to its knees this coming winter,” Jäger said. “We must expect Russian attacks of a severity and brutality that we have not yet seen on this scale. The war in Ukraine is entering a new and extremely dangerous phase.”
Jäger’s comments come a day after a politically weakened Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv in what appeared to be an attempt to show resolve following two first-place finishes by the Kremlin-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in regional elections last month. Those AfD victories, blamed in large part on the chancellor’s historically low domestic approval ratings, raised concerns in Ukraine and across the EU that German support for Ukraine might waver due to the chancellor’s troubles at home.
With his highly symbolic visit to Kyiv on Sunday, Merz sought to illustrate that he remains firmly at the helm and unflinching in his support for Ukraine.
“Mr. Putin, put an end to this senseless war,” Merz said during the visit, echoing one of his political heroes, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and his famous Cold War speech at the Brandenburg Gate alongside the Berlin Wall in 1987: “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall.”
In his comments Monday, Jäger suggested Russia’s escalation was in part driven by the fact that Putin had been backed into a corner as Moscow faces rising economic pressure and burns through resources to wage its war on Ukraine.
Putin, he said, has “passed the point where he could simply call off the attack on Ukraine without jeopardizing his domestic power base,” adding, “He must demonstrate a success in Ukraine that, from Russia’s perspective, justifies the immense sacrifices made so far.”
Jäger also said he currently sees “no evidence” for a large-scale Russian attack on a NATO member country. Yet “we consider it entirely possible that Russia might carry out targeted, smaller-scale operations” like the “little green men” who spearheaded the annexation of Crimea in 2014.

articles.title: Rubio heads to NATO allies amid threats from Russia and the war in the Middle East
articles.body:
Rubio heads to NATO allies amid threats from Russia and the war in the Middle East
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. secretary of state will visit Iceland, Greece, and Portugal from October 5–8. The sides will discuss defense, energy, Ukraine, and the Middle East.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will visit Iceland, Greece and Portugal from October 5–8, where he will hold talks on security, defense, energy, economic cooperation and technology amid growing concern among NATO countries over Russia’s military activity and instability in the Middle East. Radio Free Europe reports, writes UNN.
Details
Rubio will begin his trip in Reykjavik, where he is expected to discuss Arctic security and economic cooperation with Icelandic officials.
He will then travel to Athens for the sixth U.S.–Greece Strategic Dialogue. The agenda will include defense cooperation, energy, regional security, Ukraine and the Middle East.
The visit to Lisbon will focus on defense, economic development and technological cooperation, the U.S. Department of State said.
The three countries represent different areas of U.S. cooperation with NATO allies — from Iceland’s role in North Atlantic and Arctic security to Greece’s position in the Eastern Mediterranean and Portugal’s longstanding importance for U.S. military operations in the Atlantic.
